channel.title: Inside Desk
channel.description: A twice-daily brief on markets, geo-economics, politics, psychology and ordinary life. Optimistic by habit. Data first. Commentary, not advice.

item.title: The referees meet in the same week as the invoices
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Oil eased on Monday morning because mediators flew to Tehran. The US ten-year yield closed Friday back at 5.00%. This week three central banks set the price of money and three hyperscalers show what they spent it on.
item.content:encoded:
Oil eased on Monday morning because mediators flew to Tehran. The US ten-year yield closed Friday back at 5.00%. This week three central banks set the price of money and three hyperscalers show what they spent it on.

Monday began with a small relief and a long diary. Brent crude slipped about 1% to $115.48 a barrel in early Asian trade, after reports that Qatari mediators were in Tehran on Sunday in an effort, coordinated with the United States, to calm the region1. A later Reuters update had it 1.6% lower at $114.882. Last week Brent rose 6.2%, its highest weekly close since mid-2022, because Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia raised the fear for supply1. Those attacks did not stop over the weekend; Saudi Arabia said it intercepted drones and ballistic missiles aimed at Riyadh and the south on Sunday4. So the barrel came down a dollar or two on a flight plan, not on a ceasefire. You should price it that way too.

The long rate is the referee. The US ten-year Treasury yield closed Friday at 5.00%, according to the Treasury’s own daily curve, after 4.96% on Thursday, the lowest close since 22 September3. It peaked at 5.31% on 5 October and started the year at 4.19%3. Reuters notes that Treasuries rallied last week before “running into renewed selling on Friday”1.

That line matters more than any index. A ten-year yield of 5% is the rate against which every other promise is measured: the mortgage, the corporate bond, the data centre that pays back in 2032. When it rises, a distant profit is worth less today. When it falls, as on Thursday, the distant profit looks better and tech shares breathe. Friday’s 5.00% says the bond market has not yet decided which week it is in.

Three committees in three days. The US Federal Reserve meets from Wednesday; futures imply about a 90% chance it holds its target range at 3.75% to 4.00%6. The ECB’s Governing Council meets in Frankfurt on Wednesday and Thursday5. The Bank of Japan decides this week too6. Reuters quotes JPMorgan’s Bruce Kasman: “a relatively shallow rate hike cycle is underway”, with the big three likely on hold for now1. Markets imply about an 80% chance that the Fed moves in December, and “much the same” for the BoJ and the ECB1. New Zealand is widely expected to raise its rate on Wednesday1. A hold, in other words, is not a cut. It is a pause with the next step already in the minutes.

Three invoices. The same week, about a third of the S&P 500 reports, including Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon1. Consensus, per Reuters, is $90.6 billion of revenue for Microsoft, $202 billion for Amazon and $128 billion for Alphabet1. Their capital spending is the other half of the AI story: the bills paid to chipmakers, builders and utilities. Asia is already nervous. South Korea’s main index has shed almost a fifth of its value this month, and Japan’s Nikkei lost 4.0% last week1. Tokyo Electron fell 3.24% in early trade on Monday6.

What to do with all this. Nothing quick. The diary this week is a good one, because it is full of dull, scheduled things: decisions at fixed times, statements with numbered paragraphs, earnings reports with audited lines. The war produces headlines at random; the institutions produce documents on time. When the two disagree, the documents usually win, a little later than the headlines suggest.

The one number to watch is not an index level but the ten-year yield on Thursday evening, after the ECB and the Fed have both spoken and the first hyperscaler has shown its capital spending. If it is still near 5%, the market has heard the committees and the companies and stayed calm. If it moves sharply, someone said something that was not in the minutes. Nothing here is advice.

Sources

  1. Asian shares make cautious start, Brent eases from six-month high — Reuters via Euronext
  2. Stocks trade cautiously in Asia, Brent off six-month top — Reuters via Investing.com
  3. Daily Treasury Par Yield Curve Rates, 2026 — U.S. Department of the Treasury
  4. Saudi Arabia says it intercepted missiles and drones from Iran-backed Houthis — CNBC
  5. Weekly schedule — European Central Bank
  6. Asian Markets Today: Nikkei, Kospi fall as chip stocks drag — NDTV Profit

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: The mediators flew, the barrel slipped two dollars
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Qatar sent a delegation to Tehran on Sunday. Iran's envoy in Islamabad offered the strait for the blockade; a Revolutionary Guards outlet called a similar report 'lies and fantasy'. Brent believed the aeroplane.
item.content:encoded:
Qatar sent a delegation to Tehran on Sunday. Iran's envoy in Islamabad offered the strait for the blockade; a Revolutionary Guards outlet called a similar report 'lies and fantasy'. Brent believed the aeroplane.

Qatari mediators were in Tehran on Sunday as part of an effort to reduce regional tensions in coordination with the United States, an official briefed on the matter told Reuters1. No details of the talks were published1.

The positions around the visit were public and contradictory. Iran’s ambassador to Pakistan said on Saturday that Tehran had conveyed, through Pakistani mediators, that it was ready to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if Washington ended its blockade of Iranian ports1. The Tasnim news agency, close to the Revolutionary Guards, rejected a similar Al Arabiya report as “lies and fantasy” and said Iran “fundamentally does not accept” such an exchange1. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said a new war would not change his country’s positions2.

The market did not wait for clarity. By 0232 GMT on Monday Brent crude futures were down $2.12, or 1.82%, at $114.60, and US crude was down 2.07% at $101.133. Desk arithmetic: the drop gives back roughly a third of Friday’s gain of nearly $33.

Read that calmly. A delegation is not an agreement, and the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia went on over the weekend3. But the oil market has just told you what the conflict’s exit is worth to it: a couple of dollars on a rumour, and much more on a signature. Nothing here is advice.

Sources

  1. Qatari mediators in Tehran for US-coordinated de-escalation effort — Iran International
  2. Qatari mediators reportedly in Tehran in US-coordinated effort to ease tensions — Al Arabiya English
  3. Oil slips from near six-months highs despite supply concerns — Reuters via Investing.com

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: The court counted to 100%, and the loser said no
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Lula won Brazil's runoff with 51.79% after losing the first round, something no runner-up had done since democracy returned. Turnout did it. Flávio Bolsonaro says it is 'impossible to concede'.
item.content:encoded:
Lula won Brazil's runoff with 51.79% after losing the first round, something no runner-up had done since democracy returned. Turnout did it. Flávio Bolsonaro says it is 'impossible to concede'.

With 100% of votes counted, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva received 51.79% of the valid vote in Sunday’s runoff and Flávio Bolsonaro 48.21%1. Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, has a fourth term1. Reuters reported the result as declared by Brazil’s electoral court2.

The arithmetic of a comeback. Lula lost the first round by 2.2 million votes and won the second by 4.3 million1. Never since the return of democracy in the 1980s had the first-round runner-up won the runoff1. The Guardian points to turnout: abstention fell from a record 21.08% in the first round to 19.21%1. That is not a slogan. It is buses, polling stations and people who came back.

The refusal. Bolsonaro said it was “impossible to concede” and that his lawyers would seek to annul the election, citing a supreme court justice’s decision to extend voting by two hours to 7pm1. The Guardian notes that his own campaign had also asked the court to extend voting hours1.

The institution to watch is the dull one. Brazil counts electronically and fast; by Sunday night the result was complete1. A complaint goes to judges who work from documents. That is where a contested result should go, and where it should stay.

Sources

  1. Lula wins fourth term as Brazil president after historic upset over far-right Flávio Bolsonaro — The Guardian
  2. Asian shares make cautious start, Brent eases from six-month high — Reuters via Euronext

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Podium vs Print: "shallow" and 3.1%
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: A bank economist calls this year's rate rises shallow. Households tell the ECB they expect 3.1% inflation. Both can be right.
item.content:encoded:
A bank economist calls this year's rate rises shallow. Households tell the ECB they expect 3.1% inflation. Both can be right.

The podium. “The main message from global central banks grappling with this year’s macroeconomic surprises is that a relatively shallow rate hike cycle is underway,” JPMorgan’s Bruce Kasman said, quoted by Reuters on Monday1.

The print. In the ECB’s euro area household survey, published on Friday, expected inflation for the next 12 months rose to 3.1% from 3.0%2. Households expect the economy to shrink by 1.5% over the next year, worse than the 1.2% fall they expected in August, and unemployment to reach 11.3%2.

The gap. The economist describes interest rates; the household describes its budget: expected spending growth rose to 3.7% from 3.6% while expected income growth was only 1.1%2. Desk arithmetic: households expect their spending to grow more than three times as fast as their income. That gap is paid for with savings or credit.

The verdict. Both can be true: few, small rate rises, and households squeezed anyway. Three years out, households still expect 2.9%, as in August2. That anchor is what the central bank guards, and so far it holds.

Sources

  1. Asian shares make cautious start, Brent eases from six-month high — Reuters via Euronext
  2. ECB Consumer Expectations Survey results – September 2026 — Banque de France (ECB press release)

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Storm power at €13, Monday's back at €116
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: German onshore wind passed 1,000 GWh on both weekend days, gas burned a sixth of what it did on Wednesday, and Sunday's power cleared at €13.12. The wind is dropping, and Monday's price has climbed back.
item.content:encoded:
German onshore wind passed 1,000 GWh on both weekend days, gas burned a sixth of what it did on Wednesday, and Sunday's power cleared at €13.12. The wind is dropping, and Monday's price has climbed back.

Onshore wind turbines in Germany generated 1,009.2 gigawatt hours on Saturday and 1,019.9 GWh on Sunday, according to SMARD, the Bundesnetzagentur’s data portal1. A week earlier, on Wednesday 21 October, they made 242.3 GWh1. Gas-fired plants went the other way: 241.4 GWh on Wednesday, 42.5 GWh on Saturday and 43.5 GWh on Sunday1. Desk arithmetic: gas burned about a sixth of Wednesday’s amount. (Sunday had 25 hours, as the clocks went back.)

The auction followed the weather. The German-Luxembourg day-ahead price averaged €211.94 per megawatt hour for delivery on 21 October, €30.12 on Saturday and €13.12 on Sunday1. For Monday it is €116.571. Desk arithmetic: Monday’s power costs about nine times Sunday’s, and still about 45% less than last Wednesday’s.

The month as a whole is still dear. Over 1 to 26 October the daily price has averaged €154.41, against €85.93 over the same days of 20251. A windy weekend does not repay a month. And the Deutscher Wetterdienst expects a “transition to calm high-pressure weather” from midweek, cooling to average late-October temperatures2. Calm and cool is the combination that brings gas back into the merit order.

The lesson is not that wind is cheap on a stormy Sunday; everyone knows that. It is that the system had the turbines, the lines and the auction ready when the storm came, in the same week Brent had its best week since 2022. That is what boring, finished infrastructure looks like in a crisis. Nothing here is advice.

Sources

  1. Market data: day-ahead price DE-LU, realised generation (wind onshore, natural gas, lignite), daily — Bundesnetzagentur / SMARD.de
  2. Synoptische Übersicht Mittelfrist — Deutscher Wetterdienst

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Three committees, one pause, and the sentence after it
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: The Fed, the ECB and the Bank of Japan all decide this week, and all are expected to hold. The price of money is now set less by what they do than by what they write about December.
item.content:encoded:
The Fed, the ECB and the Bank of Japan all decide this week, and all are expected to hold. The price of money is now set less by what they do than by what they write about December.

The ECB is widely expected to leave its deposit rate at 2.5% on Thursday, after raising it in June and September as the Iran war pushed up energy prices; most economists polled by Reuters expect a quarter-point rise in December2. The Fed meets from Wednesday, and futures put the chance of an unchanged target range of 3.75% to 4.00% at about 90%4. The Bank of Japan decides this week as well4.

The decisions are not the news. Markets imply about an 80% chance of a Fed move in December, and “much the same” for the Bank of Japan and the ECB1. Goldman Sachs analysts, quoted by Reuters, expect the Fed to “skip raising rates at its October meeting” and deliver a second rise in December1. They name the risk plainly: oil futures above their forecasts1.

So this week’s real output is text. The ECB’s statement, the Fed’s statement, the press conferences. Each will either confirm December or leave it open. The bond market will read every comma, and so, a little later, will your bank’s mortgage desk.

There is dull machinery around the drama too. Before the council meets, the ECB publishes its survey on companies’ access to finance today and the Bank Lending Survey on Tuesday3. Those two papers tell the council whether its June and September rises are already reaching borrowers. They are the committee’s homework, and they arrive on time. Nothing here is advice.

Sources

  1. Asian shares make cautious start, Brent eases from six-month high — Reuters via Euronext
  2. Ready for a French test?: Five questions for the ECB — Reuters via Investing.com
  3. Weekly schedule — European Central Bank
  4. Asian Markets Today: Nikkei, Kospi fall as chip stocks drag — NDTV Profit

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Ordinary Ledger: heating oil at €174.34, and 82% say wait
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: The German average for 100 litres is €40.79 dearer than three months ago. Brent fell overnight; the heating oil price barely moved. A 3,000-litre order now costs about €5,230.
item.content:encoded:
The German average for 100 litres is €40.79 dearer than three months ago. Brent fell overnight; the heating oil price barely moved. A 3,000-litre order now costs about €5,230.

A hundred litres of heating oil cost €174.34 on the German average on Monday morning, for a 3,000-litre order, according to HeizOel241. That is 0.03% less than the day before, €3.70 more than a week ago and €40.79 more than three months ago1. The three-year range runs from €85.59 on 1 June 2025 to €179.02 on 16 September 20261.

The ledger. Desk arithmetic: a 3,000-litre delivery costs about €5,230 at today’s average, some €1,224 more than the same order three months ago and about €140 below the September high. The portal’s own rule of thumb: a litre of heating oil gives about 10 kWh, so today’s price works out at about 17.4 cents per kWh of heat1.

The exchange. At 05:18, Brent stood at $114.40 a barrel, down 0.97%, and gasoil, the wholesale product, at $1,468.25 a tonne, down 0.73%1. Only about half of what you pay comes from the oil itself; energy tax, the CO₂ levy and VAT make up much of the rest1.

The mood. In HeizOel24’s reader poll, 82% say they would wait and 18% would buy1. On Friday the “wait” side stood at 90%, by this desk’s earlier reading of the same poll. A poll is not a forecast, and an order, once placed, cannot be cancelled; the price holds until delivery, usually two to four weeks1. Nothing here is advice.

Sources

  1. Heizölpreise aktuell für Deutschland — HeizOel24
  2. Wochenvergleich: Benzinpreis gibt nach, Diesel etwas teurer, Ölpreis legt weiter zu — ADAC via Presseportal

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: SK hynix may hand back the Kioxia gain
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: A Korean newspaper says the memory maker is weighing a special dividend of about 16 trillion won, roughly $12 billion, from selling its Kioxia stake. The company says nothing is decided. Wednesday's results will say.
item.content:encoded:
A Korean newspaper says the memory maker is weighing a special dividend of about 16 trillion won, roughly $12 billion, from selling its Kioxia stake. The company says nothing is decided. Wednesday's results will say.

SK hynix is considering a special dividend of about 16 trillion won ($12 billion), funded by gains from selling its stake in the Japanese memory maker Kioxia, the South Korean newspaper Dong-A Ilbo reported on Monday1. The plan could come with third-quarter results on Wednesday1. CNBC-TV18 reported that the payout would amount to roughly 80% of the sale proceeds2. SK hynix could not be reached outside business hours, Reuters said1.

The market liked it. SK hynix shares were up 1.41% in early trade while the Kospi fell 1.00%3. Tokyo Electron fell 3.24% and Advantest 1.67%3.

Why it matters beyond Seoul: the AI trade has been an argument about whether spending will ever return cash. A memory maker handing back a one-off gain is a small, real answer: some of the boom’s profit is already in a bank account, and a board can decide to send it to shareholders. That is a duller signal than a product launch, and a more trustworthy one.

But a newspaper report is not a board decision. Wait for Wednesday’s filing.

Sources

  1. SK hynix weighs $12.1 billion special dividend, newspaper says — The Korea Herald (Reuters)
  2. Asian stocks mixed as AI sell-off, earnings and central bank meetings in focus — CNBC-TV18
  3. Asian Markets Today: Nikkei, Kospi fall as chip stocks drag — NDTV Profit

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Ebola: fewer cases a day, more deaths a day
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Congo's bulletin for 23 October counts 9,876 confirmed cases and 4,803 deaths. The seven-day average of new cases fell to 65.9 from 71.6; deaths rose to 38.1 a day from 31.6.
item.content:encoded:
Congo's bulletin for 23 October counts 9,876 confirmed cases and 4,803 deaths. The seven-day average of new cases fell to 65.9 from 71.6; deaths rose to 38.1 a day from 31.6.

The Democratic Republic of the Congo’s bulletin for 23 October reports 60 new confirmed Ebola cases and 46 deaths1. Since the Bundibugyo outbreak began there have been 9,876 confirmed cases and 4,803 deaths; 48.6% of patients have died1.

The weekly view is mixed. Over the past seven days the outbreak averaged 65.9 new cases and 38.1 deaths a day, against 71.6 cases and 31.6 deaths the week before1. No new health zone has been affected since 16 October; the outbreak remains in 66 zones across eight provinces1. Desk arithmetic: cases a day fell by about 8%, deaths a day rose by about 21%.

Of the 46 deaths, 31 happened in the community, outside a treatment centre1. That is the number to worry about: a death at home is a death the system did not reach in time, and often a body handled without protection.

The machinery is working, unevenly. Teams followed up 88.4% of contacts that day, 32,023 of 36,2181. Since 26 August, 9,415 people have received the Ervebo vaccine1. Positive tests were 13.3% of 450 samples1. None of these figures will trend online. All of them decide how this ends.

Sources

  1. DRC Ebola, 23 October 2026: 9,876 confirmed cases (SitRep 162) — Ebola Tracker, compiled from the DRC national bulletin

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Ten missiles south, two drones for Riyadh, and an airport reopened
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Saudi Arabia says it intercepted Houthi ballistic missiles, drones and a cruise missile on Sunday. The same day, Riyadh's main airport resumed operations, two weeks after the deadliest attack on the kingdom in over a decade.
item.content:encoded:
Saudi Arabia says it intercepted Houthi ballistic missiles, drones and a cruise missile on Sunday. The same day, Riyadh's main airport resumed operations, two weeks after the deadliest attack on the kingdom in over a decade.

The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said on Sunday that two drones and a ballistic missile heading for Riyadh were “intercepted and destroyed”, as were 10 ballistic missiles launched towards the kingdom’s southern region and a cruise missile aimed at Khamis Mushait1. The Houthis said they had “carried out seven qualitative military operations”, naming Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport and Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu among their targets1. Saudi Aramco did not immediately respond to CNBC1.

The airport said it was resuming operations on Sunday, using Terminal 1 for domestic flights and Terminal 2 for international routes1. It had suspended operations on 10 October after a strike that killed at least 13 people and injured around 300, the deadliest attack on Saudi Arabia in more than a decade1.

The US ordered non-emergency government staff and their families to leave Saudi Arabia last week1. Reuters reports the Houthis said they attacked the airport and oil facilities again on Saturday2.

What you can take from it: the interceptions worked on Sunday, and an airport reopened under fire. Both are the work of people doing shifts. Neither guarantees next week.

Sources

  1. Saudi Arabia says it intercepted missiles and drones from Iran-backed Houthis — CNBC
  2. Oil slips from near six-months highs despite supply concerns — Reuters via Business Recorder

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: The Rhine cleared the 2018 low by a hand
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: After four weeks below the worst day of 2018, the Kaub gauge averaged 31.3 cm on Sunday and read 52 cm at 05:15 on Monday. The weekend storm's rain is reaching the river.
item.content:encoded:
After four weeks below the worst day of 2018, the Kaub gauge averaged 31.3 cm on Sunday and read 52 cm at 05:15 on Monday. The weekend storm's rain is reaching the river.

The Rhine at Kaub, the shallowest stretch for shipping between Bingen and Koblenz, averaged 31.3 centimetres on Sunday, by this desk’s daily mean of the 15-minute readings published by the federal waterways administration1. At 05:15 on Monday the gauge read 52 cm1.

For context: the lowest daily reading of the 2010–2020 reference period was 25 cm, on 22 October 2018. From late September until Thursday this year the daily mean stayed below that line, falling below zero on several days, with a low of −4.8 cm on 1 October1. Friday’s mean of 25.9 cm put it just over; Saturday slipped back to 23.8 cm; Sunday’s 31.3 cm is the highest daily mean since at least 25 September1. Desk arithmetic: Monday’s 05:15 reading is about double the 2018 low.

The gauge number is not the water depth in the channel, which is deeper. But it is the number shippers and insurers price on. A few centimetres more at Kaub mean more tonnes per barge, fewer trips and lower freight surcharges, eventually even on heating oil delivered up the Rhine.

Do not expect a flood of relief. The Deutscher Wetterdienst expects a transition to calm high-pressure weather from midweek, with stormy gusts lingering on the North Sea on Wednesday2. Dry weeks follow storms, and the river remembers both.

Sources

  1. Kaub (Rhein), water level, 15-minute values — WSV / PEGELONLINE
  2. Synoptische Übersicht Mittelfrist — Deutscher Wetterdienst

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: The Sunday long read: the second Saturday was counted, not shouted
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: France marched again. Fewer people came, fewer marches were held, more than twice as many were arrested and the public buildings stood. The story is in the count, and the count is an institution.
item.content:encoded:
France marched again. Fewer people came, fewer marches were held, more than twice as many were arrested and the public buildings stood. The story is in the count, and the count is an institution.

Every large protest produces two numbers before it produces an argument. One comes from the Interior Ministry, the other from the unions, and the distance between them is where the evening’s television lives. On Saturday the two were 410,000 and 800,0001. Last Saturday they were 550,000 and 800,0001. The interesting fact of the week is not either number. It is that both sides kept counting, the same way, a week apart, so that you can compare them.

What the ministry counted. By its own figures, 410,000 people marched across France on 24 October in 289 actions, against 550,000 in 430 actions on 17 October1,2. In Paris the prefecture counted 110,000; the CGT said 250,0001,2. In Marseille, where a march went ahead “à titre dérogatoire”, by exception, the prefecture counted 17,000 and the CGT 100,0002. In Rennes, 11,500 people gathered despite a ban2. In Orléans, where the Rassemblement national was holding its congress, 13,500 people marched against the party and the minister reported no incidents1.

What changed. The number of arrests. By early Saturday evening the minister, Laurent Nuñez, reported “almost 1,000” arrests, and said the figure would rise “significantly” once consolidated1,3. At the same hour on 17 October the count had been 3851,3. Desk arithmetic: fewer marchers, about three quarters of last week’s, and fewer actions, about two thirds, met more than two and a half times as many arrests by the same hour. The chart above sets the three ratios side by side.

The arrests were not, mostly, made in the marches. The minister pointed to checks carried out beforehand at stations, on roads and around city centres, many on prosecutors’ requisitions, which led to seizures of objects that could be used as weapons1. That is the design announced on Friday: 70,000 police and gendarmes, 10,000 more than on 17 October; elite units guarding public buildings rather than policing marches; routes away from shopping districts preferred; prefects free to ban marches where safety could not be guaranteed4.

What it cost. Not nothing. Clashes broke out at the end of the marches in Paris, Lyon, Marseille, Rennes, Bordeaux and Toulouse2. In Paris the prefecture said more than 500 “casseurs” confronted police on the cours de Vincennes, for at least two hours by the minister’s account2. Two people were seriously injured, in Toulouse and Clermont-Ferrand, and 22 were hurt in Lyon, 18 of them police officers5. In Marseille three shops were looted or damaged2. The minister spoke of an “extremely high level of violence”2. Those are real injuries and real shop windows, and they deserve inquiries, not adjectives.

But compare the week before. On 17 October the evening was looting and the morning was a list of damaged towns. On Saturday the minister’s summary was a sentence a ministry rarely gets to say: “Les cortèges se sont bien passés”, the marches went well, and the public buildings stood2,3. The CGT’s leader, Sophie Binet, called it “a massive and peaceful mobilisation despite provocations”2. The minister and the union disagreed, as usual, on the number. They agreed, unusually, on the character of the march itself.

The Friday in between. The week was not calm. On Friday morning a gunman opened fire from a car in Trappes and La Verrière, west of Paris, killing one person and wounding others, among them a 12-year-old girl6. A 39-year-old suspect was arrested the same day, and the national anti-terrorism prosecutor opened an investigation6. This desk still waits for the prosecutor on motive. What matters here is sequence: an attack in the morning, an arrest the same day, and the next day’s marches held. A state under strain that keeps doing its paperwork in the right order is a state that works.

The contrarian half. The loudest reading of the week was that France is coming apart. The counts say something duller and more hopeful. Whichever count you prefer, hundreds of thousands of people walked through their cities to complain about prices and public services, and the overwhelming majority walked home. The violence moved from the middle of the day to the end of it, and the police met it earlier, at stations and on approach roads, under prosecutors’ warrants.

It is not a victory. The measure of the policing will be how many of those arrests hold up before a judge, and whether the two serious injuries are explained. The right to march is only protected if the people who police it are accountable for how they do it.

What this means for you. When the next protest weekend comes, wait for the second number: the same figure, from the same counter, a week later. The change in a series tells you more than the size of a headline.

The constructive reading. A government asked to choose between order and the right to protest chose to publish its plan the day before, count its arrests in public and compare them with last week’s. Unions counted their own marchers and said so. A prosecutor took the attack, so that nobody else had to guess. None of that is heroic. It is the dull machinery that lets a country argue about the price of diesel without burning down the shop that sells it.

Sources

  1. Mobilisation en baisse, près de 1 000 interpellations, deux blessés graves… Ce qu'il faut retenir de cette nouvelle journée de manifestation contre la vie chère — franceinfo
  2. Mobilisation suivie et défilés dans le calme, heurts en fin de cortèges... Le point sur les manifestations du 24 octobre — TF1 Info
  3. Cortège calme, 1.000 interpellations, bâtiments publics intacts: Laurent Nuñez tire son bilan des manifestations du 24 octobre — BFMTV
  4. Blindés, unités d'élite, 70 000 policiers et gendarmes… Laurent Nuñez détaille l'important dispositif de sécurité mobilisé pour les manifestations du 24 octobre — franceinfo
  5. EN DIRECT Mobilisation du 24 octobre : près de 1 000 interpellations, plusieurs blessés graves… Les dernières infos au lendemain des manifestations — Midi Libre
  6. Un mort et plusieurs blessés graves, un suspect arrêté, "un crime terroriste"... Ce que l'on sait de l'attaque à l'arme à feu à Trappes et La Verrière — franceinfo

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: The Sunday Sequence: the week in the order it was priced
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Chips fell first, bonds caught them second, oil rose third and the rest of the market paid fourth. The S&P 500 lost half a per cent on the week. The sequence is the lesson; the half per cent is not.
item.content:encoded:
Chips fell first, bonds caught them second, oil rose third and the rest of the market paid fourth. The S&P 500 lost half a per cent on the week. The sequence is the lesson; the half per cent is not.

On Sundays this desk puts the week back in order. Not by size of headline, but in the order in which prices moved, because the order tells you which worry was driving and which was being dragged along.

1. The chips went first. On Thursday the Philadelphia semiconductor index fell almost 7% and the Nasdaq 2.6%, its worst day since June1. The worry was not demand. It was the cost of borrowing to meet it: data centres are increasingly paid for with debt, and debt has a price1.

2. The bonds caught them. The same day investors ran to US government bonds, giving Treasuries their biggest rally in more than three years1. Almost a full quarter-point of Fed rate rises for next year was priced out during the week1. When one half of a balanced portfolio falls and the other rises, that is not luck. That is the design.

3. Oil rose third, and hardest. On Friday Brent settled at $116.72 a barrel, up $3.55 on the day and 6.24% on the week, its highest settlement since 29 April2,3. Dow Jones Market Data counts five weekly gains in a row and a rise of 12.74% so far this month3. WTI settled at $103.272. Reuters tied Friday’s move to Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia and an oil spill off the UAE2.

4. Everyone else paid fourth. On Friday the Dow fell 652.82 points, or 1.23%, to 52,215.16; the S&P 500 lost 0.52% to 7,623.68; the Nasdaq slipped 0.21%4. Technology steadied, rising 0.35%, while consumer staples, consumer discretionary and financials each fell more than 1%4. American Express fell more than 3% after announcing it would cut about 5% of its global workforce, citing the need to “prepare for AI”5. On the week, the S&P 500 lost 0.5% and the Nasdaq 0.7%, while the Dow gained 0.4%, its third weekly gain in a row4.

What the order says. The week began as a technology story and ended as an oil story. By Friday the selling had moved from the companies that build the future to the companies that sell groceries and lend money today, which is what a higher fuel bill does: it taxes everything a little. “There is still fallout from the questioning of the AI trade,” Kristina Hooper of Man Group told Reuters4. True, and by Friday it was no longer the main fallout.

What it does not say. It does not say a crash has begun. A half-per-cent weekly loss after a seven-per-cent day in chips is a market absorbing news, not panicking about it. The harder test arrives this week, when about a third of S&P 500 companies report, among them Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon4. Their capital-spending forecasts are the invoice the whole AI trade is waiting to read.

For you. If you hold a broad fund, this was a week in which it did what it says on the tin. Nothing here is advice.

Sources

  1. Tech selloff relents, oil at five-month high — Reuters via Investing.com
  2. Oil prices jump $3 on Houthi attacks, oil spill, highest settlement since April — Reuters via Investing.com
  3. Front Month ICE Brent Crude Rose 6.24% This Week to Settle at $116.72 — Data Talk — Dow Jones Market Data via Morningstar
  4. Wall Street closes lower to end rocky week — Reuters via Investing.com
  5. Stock market news for Oct. 23, 2026 — CNBC

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Podium vs Print: "Absolutely" and $116.72
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: An ambassador said a strike could come this weekend, his president said he knew nothing about it, and an Iranian envoy said Tehran was still open to talks. The oil market did not wait to find out who was right.
item.content:encoded:
An ambassador said a strike could come this weekend, his president said he knew nothing about it, and an Iranian envoy said Tehran was still open to talks. The oil market did not wait to find out who was right.

The podium, in three voices. On Friday Tom Barrack, the US ambassador to Türkiye, was asked whether there could be a US strike on Iran this weekend. “Absolutely,” he said, while adding that President Trump remained open to a diplomatic agreement and that efforts involving Pakistan and Qatar were under way1. Asked about it after landing in Florida, the president said: “If that’s the case, I don’t know anything about it”1. On Saturday Iran’s ambassador to Pakistan, Reza Amiri Moghadam, said Tehran remained open to talks under the interim deal Pakistan brokered in June, and that it had told Washington through Pakistan it was prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if the US lifted its naval blockade3.

Then the fourth voice. Iran’s armed-forces chief, Major General Ali Abdollahi, said Iran would “under no circumstances and at no time” allow US military vessels into the Persian Gulf1. The IRGC’s navy claimed that two supertankers carrying more than 4.5 million barrels between them had struck mines on what it called an unauthorised route; the claim could not be independently verified1.

The print. The oil market voted on Friday afternoon, New York time, before Saturday’s statements were made. Brent settled at $116.72, up 6.24% on the week, the largest weekly gain since the week ending 11 September and the fifth weekly rise in a row2. It was the highest settlement since 29 April, and just 1.38% below this year’s settlement high of $118.35 on 31 March2. Al Jazeera put the week’s move down to continued attacks on ships in and around the strait together with “the increased odds of renewed war”4.

The gap. The podiums disagree with each other. An ambassador says yes, his president says he does not know, an envoy says talks, a general says never. You cannot average those into a forecast, and this desk will not try. What you can do is notice that the print does not need to know which of them is right. It prices the probability that any of them is, and it does so in dollars.

What the print does not tell you. A futures price is a bet on the next few weeks, not a measure of how much oil actually moves. The physical picture comes from ship counts and port data, and those are patchy in a war: some tankers cross with their transponders off. The $116.72 says the market is paying for risk. It does not say how much oil is missing.

Verdict. The podium offered four positions in two days. The print offered one number, settled and published, with a weekly change you can check. On a weekend of strike talk and talks talk, the dull rule holds: when officials disagree, read the price they are all trying to move. Nothing here is advice.

Sources

  1. Iran claims Strait of Hormuz control, warns US warships against entering Persian Gulf amid fresh strike threat — The Economic Times (ANI)
  2. Front Month ICE Brent Crude Rose 6.24% This Week to Settle at $116.72 — Data Talk — Dow Jones Market Data via Morningstar
  3. Iran remains open to talks with US under Pakistan-brokered deal, envoy says — The Washington Post (AP)
  4. Iran says won't allow US warships to get close as Trump ponders new attacks — Al Jazeera

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: One candidate, and 98.98 per cent
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: The Rassemblement national re-elected its president in Orléans with no opponent. In Berlin the Länder asked for a tax cut with no funding line. Both are votes; only one of them was counted.
item.content:encoded:
The Rassemblement national re-elected its president in Orléans with no opponent. In Berlin the Länder asked for a tax cut with no funding line. Both are votes; only one of them was counted.

Orléans. Jordan Bardella, the only candidate, was re-elected president of the Rassemblement national at the party’s congress in Orléans on Saturday with 98.98% of the votes cast1,2. That was 75,497 votes, against 779 blank ballots, on a turnout of about 68%1,2. Members had voted electronically from 21 September to 22 October1,2. Outside, 13,500 people marched against the party, and the Interior Ministry reported no incidents3.

What the number measures. Not popularity in the country. A single-candidate vote tells you two things: how many members bothered to vote, and how few chose to spoil their ballot. About a third did not vote at all1. Desk arithmetic: of members entitled to vote, roughly two in three said yes. That is a strong showing for discipline and a weak one for drama, which may be exactly what the party wanted.

Berlin, the same week. On Thursday the sixteen state premiers asked the federal government to cut the electricity tax for everyone “as quickly as possible”4. On Friday the deputy government spokesman said the goal stands, “under a financing proviso”, and named no date4. Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil had said that anyone proposing a cut should bring proposals for how to pay for it4.

The common thread. Both stories are about the difference between a mandate and a ledger. A party can give its leader 98.98% in a month of voting. A coalition can agree a goal in a single sentence. Neither has yet said where the money for its promises comes from, and that is the question voters in both countries face at the till this autumn.

The constructive reading. Both systems are doing the dull part properly. A party published its vote count, blank ballots included. A federal spokesman said out loud that a tax cut needs funding. Neither is exciting. Both are the kind of sentence you can hold someone to later.

Sources

  1. Au congrès du Rassemblement national, l'unique candidat Jordan Bardella est réélu sans surprise à la présidence du parti avec 98,98% des voix — franceinfo
  2. Congrès du RN : un plébiscite pour Jordan Bardella, réélu à la tête du parti avec 98,98% des voix — Euronews
  3. Mobilisation en baisse, près de 1 000 interpellations, deux blessés graves… Ce qu'il faut retenir de cette nouvelle journée de manifestation contre la vie chère — franceinfo
  4. Bundesregierung sagt trotz Drängens der Länder keine schnelle Stromsteuersenkung zu — Reuters via onvista

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: The mood moves in a fortnight, the till in a season
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: British confidence fell by the most since the first lockdown. British shoppers bought a little less. A market strategist called the AI trade a bubble and then said that was fine. This week was a lesson in reading feelings next to behaviour.
item.content:encoded:
British confidence fell by the most since the first lockdown. British shoppers bought a little less. A market strategist called the AI trade a bubble and then said that was fine. This week was a lesson in reading feelings next to behaviour.

The feeling. GfK’s consumer confidence index for Britain fell eleven points to −24 in October, the biggest monthly drop since April 20201. Outside the pandemic, the last fall on that scale followed the 2016 Brexit vote1. “The speed of this deterioration is alarming,” said Neil Bellamy of GfK1. The survey asked 2,003 adults between 1 and 14 October1.

The behaviour. The Office for National Statistics reported that retail sales volumes fell 0.4% in September, after a 0.7% rise in August; over the third quarter they still rose 0.7%2. Fuel volumes rose on the month “despite fuel prices continuing to rise”2. People said they felt much worse; they spent a little less.

Why that is normal. Surveys capture expectations, and expectations move as fast as the evening news. Spending is made of routines: the weekly shop, the commute, the tank that has to be filled whatever the price. Routines change slowly and partly. That is why a confidence survey is a warning light, not a verdict, and why the honest answer to “are people cutting back?” is usually “a little, and later”.

The kind word. On Thursday, after chip stocks fell almost 7%, the strategist Ed Yardeni called the AI trade a “bubble”, and then added: “Taking some air out of the AI bubble is a good thing. I don’t think it’s going to burst and create problems for the economy”3. Words travel in families. “Bubble” usually comes with “burst” and “panic”. Here it came with “maintenance”. You do not have to agree with him to notice which framing is easier to think with.

For you. When the news says everyone feels poorer, look at your own bank statement before you change your plans. It is the one series you can read every day, and it is usually calmer than the headline. Nothing here is advice.

Sources

  1. UK consumer confidence tumbles ahead of Healey's budget, GfK reports — Reuters via Investing.com
  2. Retail sales, Great Britain: September 2026 — Office for National Statistics
  3. Dow tumbles more than 800 points as Middle East tensions rise, selling broadens beyond tech: Live updates — CNBC

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: The Annex: a refinery paper and a two-section regulation
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Berlin did two things about fuel this week. One was a dialogue with a strategy to follow. The other was a regulation that lends the market eight days of the national oil reserve. Read both, line by line.
item.content:encoded:
Berlin did two things about fuel this week. One was a dialogue with a strategy to follow. The other was a regulation that lends the market eight days of the national oil reserve. Read both, line by line.

Document one: the refinery release. On Friday the economy ministry opened a dialogue with the mineral-oil industry on the future of Germany’s refineries, to be turned into a strategy paper for the cabinet1. Line by line:

  • The inventory. Eleven refinery sites, a processing capacity of a little over 92 million tonnes of crude a year1. This is the most useful sentence in the release, because it is a count.
  • The claim. The loss of these sites “cannot be compensated by imports” and would threaten the chemical companies that depend on them1. A strong sentence. It is an argument, not yet a finding.
  • The bill. The plants must convert step by step to sustainable feedstocks, which needs “investments in the billions”1. The release does not say whose billions.
  • The method. A cross-ministry study on what a resilient energy system needs, and how resilience can be anchored in planning and administration1. Count, then study, then decide: the correct order, and a slow one.

Document two: the reserve regulation. The seventh regulation on releasing stocks of Germany’s oil stockholding agency took effect on Thursday2,3. Line by line:

  • The number. The agency may temporarily reduce its required stock from 90 days of cover to 822,3. Eight days of national cover are being lent to the market.
  • The share. Under the International Energy Agency’s key, Germany contributes 19.5 million of a 100-million-barrel release; 6 million had been released by October2.
  • The order. For the remaining 13.5 million barrels, the ministry will start with diesel and heating oil2. Those are the products that fill the tank and the boiler.
  • The length. Two sections, with the consent of the Bundesrat3. Brevity is a virtue in a regulation.

Reading them together. The first document is about the 2030s; the second is about November. One has a study attached, the other a number of days. On a week when Brent settled at $116.72, its highest since April4, it was the shorter text that put barrels where people buy them.

The constructive reading. Neither document is dramatic. Both begin with a count, sites and tonnes in one, days and barrels in the other. A state that knows what it has before it decides what to do is doing energy policy the dull, right way round. Nothing here is advice.

Sources

  1. Bundesregierung startet Raffineriestrategie: Resilienz stärken, Wettbewerbsfähigkeit sichern, Transformation ermöglichen — Bundesministerium für Wirtschaft und Energie (BMWE)
  2. Bundesregierung gibt weiteren Teil der Ölreserve frei — WirtschaftsWoche
  3. Siebte Verordnung über die Freigabe von Vorräten des Erdölbevorratungsverbandes (7. ErdölFrV) — gesetze-im-internet.de
  4. Oil prices jump $3 on Houthi attacks, oil spill, highest settlement since April — Reuters via Investing.com

item.title: Seventy of seventy-three, and a survey that agreed
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Economists expect the ECB to hold on Thursday. The week's business survey gave them a reason: costs up, selling prices slower. A committee that waits for the second print is not dithering; it is reading.
item.content:encoded:
Economists expect the ECB to hold on Thursday. The week's business survey gave them a reason: costs up, selling prices slower. A committee that waits for the second print is not dithering; it is reading.

The poll. In a Reuters survey taken from 5 to 8 October, all but three of 73 economists expected the European Central Bank to hold its deposit rate at 2.50% at its meeting ending on Thursday 29 October; 64 expected a quarter-point rise in December1. Inflation was 3.8% in September, nearly double the 2% target1. Economists expected it to average 3.7% this quarter1.

The argument for waiting. The poll named it: so far there has been “scant evidence” that higher energy prices are spilling into other consumer prices, which would be the trigger for further rises1. “Market rates have increased meaningfully and are doing some of the job for the ECB,” said Anatoli Annenkov of Société Générale1.

The week’s evidence. On Friday the flash composite PMI for the euro area fell to 51.9 in October from 53.1, below every forecast in a Reuters poll2. France fell back into contraction; Germany slowed but kept growing2. Inside the survey was the line committees read first: input costs rose faster for a second month, driven by energy, fuel and transport, while firms raised their own selling prices more slowly than in September2. “There is still little evidence of second-round effects, which will be reassuring for the ECB,” said Harry Chambers of Capital Economics2.

The bond market’s vote. French ten-year yields rose nearly 27 basis points over the week to about 5.05% on Friday, and the spread over German Bunds stayed above 170 basis points, its widest since the euro-zone debt crisis3. Desk arithmetic: 170 basis points is 1.7 percentage points a year on every euro France borrows for ten years. That is tightening, of a kind, delivered without a meeting.

What to expect, without forecasting. This desk does not forecast decisions. It reads what a committee is looking at. On Thursday it will be looking at costs rising, prices following slowly, wages not yet moving and one large member state’s borrowing cost rising on its own. That is a list that argues for patience, and for keeping the next step open.

For you. If you are fixing a mortgage or a savings rate this autumn, the price that matters is the market rate your bank quotes, which already moved. The committee’s decision on Thursday is the second print, not the first. Nothing here is advice.

Sources

  1. ECB to hike rates again in December as inflation almost doubles 2% target: Reuters poll — Reuters via Investing.com
  2. Euro zone growth slows to 4-month low amid rising costs and French strife, survey shows — Reuters via Investing.com
  3. Tech selloff relents, oil at five-month high — Reuters via Investing.com

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Ordinary Ledger: the storm sold power at €13, the tank still cost €112
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Germany's wholesale electricity price fell from €211.94 on Wednesday to €13.12 for Sunday as the wind picked up. Diesel at the pump barely moved. Two invoices, one weekend, and only one of them reaches you this month.
item.content:encoded:
Germany's wholesale electricity price fell from €211.94 on Wednesday to €13.12 for Sunday as the wind picked up. Diesel at the pump barely moved. Two invoices, one weekend, and only one of them reaches you this month.

The Ordinary Ledger reads the week’s prices in the order a household meets them. This week two of them went in opposite directions, and only one moved fast.

Power, wholesale. Germany’s day-ahead electricity auction cleared at a daily average of €211.94 per megawatt hour for Wednesday, then €148.61 for Thursday, €137.59 for Friday, €30.12 for Saturday and €13.12 for Sunday1. Desk arithmetic: Sunday’s power costs about one sixteenth of Wednesday’s.

Why. The weather, not a minister. Onshore wind turbines generated 242,281 megawatt hours on Wednesday and 1,009,174 on Saturday; gas-fired plants fell from 241,432 to 42,4562. Desk arithmetic: wind about four times higher, gas down to about a sixth. When the wind supplies most of the demand, the expensive gas plant no longer sets the price, and the auction clears low.

Why you will not see it this month. One windy weekend is not a cheap month. Over 1 to 25 October the day-ahead price averaged €155.92, against €89.11 over the same days of 20251. Desk arithmetic: about three quarters higher. Most households pay a tariff their supplier bought months ahead. The wholesale line is next year’s weather report, not this month’s bill.

Fuel, at the pump. ADAC’s weekly reading on Wednesday put Super E10 at €2.110 a litre, down 4.1 cents on the week, and diesel at €2.255, up 0.8 cents3. ADAC said most of the tax cut now appears to be reaching petrol pumps3. Desk arithmetic: a 50-litre diesel tank cost about €112.75, a 50-litre E10 tank about €105.50. Brent rose 6% after that reading was taken, so the next one may not be as kind.

Heating oil. On Friday afternoon the German average stood at €174.25 per 100 litres, €4.96 more than a week earlier and €40.21 more than three months earlier4. No wind farm helps a tank in the cellar.

The ledger, totalled. Down sharply: wholesale power, for a weekend. Down a little: petrol. Up a little: diesel. Up steadily: heating oil. The fast-moving price was the one you mostly do not pay directly; the ones you do pay moved slowly, and mostly up.

The constructive reading. Every number here was free and public by Sunday morning: an auction result and a generation count from the regulator’s own platform, a weekly pump average, a daily heating-oil price. You can see your winter coming in more detail than any household could a generation ago. Nothing here is advice.

Sources

  1. Day-ahead price DE-LU, daily (filter 4169) — Bundesnetzagentur | SMARD.de
  2. Realised generation, wind onshore (filter 4067) and natural gas (filter 4071), Germany, daily — Bundesnetzagentur | SMARD.de
  3. Tanken in Deutschland: Benzinpreis sinkt, Dieselpreis steigt leicht — ADAC
  4. Heizölpreise aktuell für Deutschland — HeizOel24

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: The hyperscalers send their invoices this week
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: After a week of keynotes, chip sell-offs and a card company cutting jobs "to prepare for AI", the numbers that matter arrive from Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon. Read the capital-spending line first.
item.content:encoded:
After a week of keynotes, chip sell-offs and a card company cutting jobs "to prepare for AI", the numbers that matter arrive from Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon. Read the capital-spending line first.

The week behind. On Thursday chip stocks had one of their worst days of the year, and the Nasdaq its worst day since June, as investors worried about the cost of financing the data-centre build-out1. Dario Perkins of TS Lombard summed up the shift for CNBC: until recently the hyperscalers invested out of cash flow, but now “debt is now the marginal source of funding”3. On Friday technology shares steadied; the sector rose 0.35% while the wider market fell1.

Two smaller stories with the same moral. American Express shares fell more than 3% after the company said it would cut about 5% of its global workforce, citing the need to “prepare for AI”2. And telecoms fell hard: AT&T and T-Mobile both sank nearly 8% after a report that SpaceX was seeking thousands of cell sites for a fourth wireless carrier, while tower owners rose, Crown Castle by 9%1. One story is about the claim that software replaces people; the other about a rocket company needing very ordinary steel masts on roofs. Both end in physical, countable things: payrolls and towers.

The week ahead. About a third of S&P 500 companies report, including Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon, “three AI hyperscalers whose capital spending forecasts will be closely watched”, as Reuters put it1. That line is the invoice of the whole AI economy. Chipmakers, power utilities, transformer makers, electricians: their order books are a share of it.

How to read them. Three numbers, in order. Capital spending, and whether it is rising or flattening. Operating cash flow, and whether it covers that spending. New debt, and at what rate. Revenue growth is the headline; the cash-flow statement is the story. A company can report record sales and still be borrowing to build.

The constructive reading. For two years the AI trade was priced on speeches. It is now priced on financing costs, which is a sign of a market growing up. Boring questions about who pays, from which account, at what interest rate, are the ones that keep a boom from becoming a bust. Nothing here is advice.

Sources

  1. Wall Street closes lower to end rocky week — Reuters via Investing.com
  2. Stock market news for Oct. 23, 2026 — CNBC
  3. Emerging credit risk: What could take out the AI trade — CNBC

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Ebola: a list, one name at a time
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Congo passed 9,700 confirmed cases. Kenya traced all but one of 135 contacts to quarantine. Europe's disease agency said screening at airports would not work and clear information would. A week of grim numbers and correct method.
item.content:encoded:
Congo passed 9,700 confirmed cases. Kenya traced all but one of 135 contacts to quarantine. Europe's disease agency said screening at airports would not work and clear information would. A week of grim numbers and correct method.

The count. As of 21 October the Democratic Republic of the Congo had reported 9,704 confirmed cases of Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus, including 4,687 deaths, in data up to 20 October1. In the latest reporting interval there were 67 new confirmed cases and 41 deaths, in Ituri, North Kivu and Tshopo1. Ituri remains the centre, with 7,040 cases1. 2,595 people who tested positive have recovered1. ECDC says the outbreak is probably larger than reported, because of gaps in data and contact follow-up1.

Beyond Congo. Kenya has nine confirmed cases, including one death, all linked to a first case imported from Congo; 134 of 135 contacts are in quarantine1. Nigeria reported its first case on 20 October, a woman who flew in from Uganda, and 44 close contacts are being monitored1.

What Europe was told. ECDC rates the likelihood of infection as very low for people living in the EU and EEA1. It also said something that runs against instinct: screening returning travellers “would not be effective” in keeping the virus out, judging from the 2013–2016 West African outbreak1. What works is giving travellers clear information on symptoms and on what to do if they fall ill after arrival1. That is a less visible policy than a thermometer at the gate, and a better one.

What is missing. There is no licensed vaccine or specific treatment for Bundibugyo virus1. Congo began vaccinating frontline workers in August with Ervebo, made for a different Ebola species, mainly within research protocols1.

Closer to home. WHO Europe reminded the region on Friday that the flu season usually starts between mid-November and mid-December2. It recommends annual vaccination for older people, pregnant women, young children, people with chronic conditions and health workers, because last year’s protection wanes and the vaccine is updated each year2.

The constructive reading. The Ebola numbers are grim, and they are numbers: published, broken down by health zone, compared week on week. Kenya found 134 of 135 contacts. That is what a working response looks like. The flu advice is the same idea at a smaller scale: a known season, a known vaccine, a date to book. Nothing here is medical advice; ask your doctor.

Sources

  1. Ebola disease outbreak caused by Bundibugyo virus – Multi-country – 2026 (update of 22 October) — European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC)
  2. Get ready for this year's influenza season: vaccination is key — WHO Regional Office for Europe

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Boelo blew the price down; the Rhine barely rose
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: The season's second named storm brought 85 mph gusts to Britain and near-free power to Germany. The Rhine at Kaub touched the 2018 low line for a day, then slipped back under it. One weather system, three ledgers.
item.content:encoded:
The season's second named storm brought 85 mph gusts to Britain and near-free power to Germany. The Rhine at Kaub touched the 2018 low line for a day, then slipped back under it. One weather system, three ledgers.

The storm. Boelo, the second named storm of the season, reached Britain on Saturday after Austen on Friday1,2. The BBC reported gusts of 85 mph overnight at Machrihanish in western Scotland and at The Needles off the Isle of Wight1. Amber wind warnings covered Scotland, the far north of England and parts of Northern Ireland into Sunday1. Trains and ferries were cancelled in Scotland, and dozens of flood warnings and alerts were in place1. As of 06:30 on Sunday, National Grid said 10,860 properties still had no electricity; on Saturday it said more than 124,000 had been reconnected since the storms began1.

The power price. The same weather system blew across the North Sea. Germany’s onshore wind turbines generated 1,009,174 megawatt hours on Saturday, roughly four times Wednesday’s 242,2814. The day-ahead electricity price fell to €30.12 for Saturday and €13.12 for Sunday, from €211.94 on Wednesday4. Our Ordinary Ledger has the arithmetic, and why it will not reach your bill this month.

The river. The Rhine at Kaub, the Middle Rhine gauge that barge operators watch, spent four weeks below 25 centimetres, the lowest daily reading of the 2010–2020 reference period, set on 22 October 20183. On Friday its daily mean of 15-minute readings reached 25.9 cm, just above that line; on Saturday it was back to 23.8 cm3. By 08:45 on Sunday it read 27 cm3. Desk arithmetic: the daily means are averages of the published 15-minute values.

Why the storm did not fill the river. Boelo’s warnings, for wind and for rain, were for Britain and Ireland1,2. The Rhine is fed from the Alps, the Black Forest and the hills along its course. A storm can make the news in Glasgow and leave the gauge in Kaub almost where it was. That is why this desk reads the gauge, not the weather map.

The constructive reading. Three ledgers, three honest numbers: homes reconnected in Britain, megawatt hours of wind in Germany, centimetres of water at Kaub. Each was published by a public body, for free, within hours. Weather cannot be managed. Its bills can be read in advance, and that is most of what preparation is.

Sources

  1. Storm Boelo hits UK with gusts up to 85mph gusts as amber warnings hold — BBC News
  2. Warnings in place as Storm Boelo to impact UK — Met Office
  3. PEGELONLINE REST API: Kaub (Rhein), water level W, 15-minute raw values — Wasserstraßen- und Schifffahrtsverwaltung des Bundes (WSV)
  4. Day-ahead price DE-LU, daily (filter 4169); realised generation, wind onshore (filter 4067) — Bundesnetzagentur | SMARD.de

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: The wind paid for Friday. The tank did not.
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Wholesale power for Friday cleared at €137.59, a third below Wednesday, because the wind came back. Heating oil rose to €174.25 because Brent did. Your winter has two meters, and only one of them blows in from the North Sea.
item.content:encoded:
Wholesale power for Friday cleared at €137.59, a third below Wednesday, because the wind came back. Heating oil rose to €174.25 because Brent did. Your winter has two meters, and only one of them blows in from the North Sea.

Two prices reached German households on Friday, and they moved in opposite directions.

The first is the wholesale price of electricity. Friday’s day-ahead auction for Germany and Luxembourg cleared at an average of €137.59 per megawatt hour, after €148.61 for Thursday and €211.94 for Wednesday1. Desk arithmetic: Friday is 35% cheaper than Wednesday.

Why it fell. No minister did this. The weather did. Onshore wind turbines generated 673,227 megawatt hours on Thursday, against 242,281 on Wednesday, and gas-fired plants dropped from 241,432 to 123,316 megawatt hours2. Desk arithmetic: wind nearly tripled, gas halved. When the wind blows, the most expensive plant needed to meet demand is less often a gas turbine, and the whole auction clears lower.

Why it is still dear. One windy day does not make a cheap month. Over 1 to 23 October the day-ahead price averaged €167.60, against €94.97 over the same days of 20251. Desk arithmetic: about three quarters higher. September averaged €144.821. Most households do not pay the day-ahead price directly; their supplier buys ahead and passes costs on later. The wholesale line is the weather report for next year’s tariff, not this month’s bill.

The second price. Heating oil climbed to a German average of €174.25 per 100 litres on Friday, 0.90% more than Thursday, €4.96 more than a week ago and €40.21 more than three months ago3. It follows crude, and crude followed the war: Brent touched $115.16 in London trading, its highest since 4 May, after Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and reports of plans for renewed strikes on Iran4. No wind farm helps a tank in the cellar.

The promise in the middle. On Thursday the sixteen state premiers asked Berlin to cut the electricity tax “as quickly as possible”. On Friday the deputy government spokesman said the goal stands, but “under a financing proviso”, and named no date5. Our Politics desk weighs that promise against its price tonight.

What this means for you. Three things are worth separating. A windy week lowers the wholesale price you mostly do not pay yet. A war lowers nothing; it raises the oil and gas prices you pay directly, quickly. A tax cut lowers a bill only after it is law, financed and passed on. None of the three is in your hands. What is in your hands is the reading on your own meter and the size of your own order. Those numbers do not care about speeches.

The constructive reading. Every number in this piece was public and free by Friday afternoon: an auction result from the regulator’s own platform, a generation count by fuel, a daily price average from thousands of orders1,2,3. A household in 2026 can see its winter coming in better detail than a utility could twenty years ago. That is not comfort. It is information, and information is the start of a plan. Nothing here is advice.

Sources

  1. Day-ahead price DE-LU, daily (filter 4169) — Bundesnetzagentur | SMARD.de
  2. Realised generation, wind onshore (filter 4067) and natural gas (filter 4071), Germany, daily — Bundesnetzagentur | SMARD.de
  3. Heizölpreise aktuell für Deutschland — HeizOel24
  4. Brent crude hits more than five-month high on Houthi-Saudi attacks, UAE oil spill — Reuters via Investing.com
  5. Bundesregierung sagt trotz Drängens der Länder keine schnelle Stromsteuersenkung zu — Reuters via onvista

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Oil bought the war, bonds bought the fear
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Brent touched a five-month high, US crude stayed above $100 and the Dow fell 600 points. The ten-year Treasury yield, which had its biggest one-day fall since 2023 on Thursday, stayed just under 5%. Two scares, two different shelters.
item.content:encoded:
Brent touched a five-month high, US crude stayed above $100 and the Dow fell 600 points. The ten-year Treasury yield, which had its biggest one-day fall since 2023 on Thursday, stayed just under 5%. Two scares, two different shelters.

Friday had two stories, and they asked investors for opposite things.

The oil story. Brent crude futures reached $115.16 a barrel in London, the highest since 4 May, and stood at $114.99 by 13:00 GMT; US crude was at $101.272. Reuters had Brent on course for a 4.4% weekly rise, its third in a row, while WTI was on track for a small weekly fall2. The reasons are listed in the copy, not in the charts: Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, an oil spill off the UAE, and reports that Washington and Israel have drawn up plans for renewed strikes on Iran after the US midterm elections2,3.

The stock story. On Wall Street the Dow fell about 600 points in early trade, while the Nasdaq barely moved, a sign, the Wall Street Journal noted, that the AI rout of Thursday might be easing4. CNBC had the S&P 500 down 0.6% at the open and the Dow down 1.3%1. Thursday’s selling had sent the Philadelphia semiconductor index down almost 7% and the Nasdaq down 2.6%, its worst day since June3.

The shelter. On Thursday investors ran to US government bonds, giving Treasuries their biggest rally in more than three years3. On Friday the ten-year yield edged up to 4.97%, still just under 5%1. The VIX, the options market’s gauge of expected volatility, rose another 6% to 20.241. Almost a full quarter-point of Fed hikes for next year has been priced out this week3.

Elsewhere. Asia closed mixed. The Nikkei lost 0.34%, Korea’s Kospi gained 0.3%, and China’s CSI 300 rose 1.71% but still closed lower for the week for an eleventh straight time1. Europe was 0.5% lower before New York opened3.

What to make of it. The two stories do not cancel out. Oil rose on a risk that may or may not arrive. Tech fell on a cost, the cost of borrowing to build data centres, that has already arrived. If you hold a broad fund, Friday reminded you why it holds both stocks and bonds: on Thursday one went down while the other went up. That is the boring design doing its job. Nothing here is advice.

Sources

  1. Stocks open lower as U.S. oil tops $100 amid escalating Iran tensions: Live updates — CNBC
  2. Brent crude hits more than five-month high on Houthi-Saudi attacks, UAE oil spill — Reuters via Investing.com
  3. Tech selloff relents, oil at five-month high — Reuters via Investing.com
  4. Stock Market Today: Dow Slides as Oil Prices Climb to Highest in Five Months — The Wall Street Journal

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Podium vs Print: "more oil than before" and six ships
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: The US president says more oil now passes Hormuz than before the war. The public ship counter logged six commercial crossings on Thursday, against a pre-war baseline of 84.8 a day. Both cannot be the whole picture.
item.content:encoded:
The US president says more oil now passes Hormuz than before the war. The public ship counter logged six commercial crossings on Thursday, against a pre-war baseline of 84.8 a day. Both cannot be the whole picture.

The podium. On Thursday President Trump accused Iran of trying to push up oil prices before the midterm elections. “They are making up fake hits, mines, and everything else,” he wrote, “because more oil is coming through the Hormuz Strait now than it did even prior to the beginning of the conflict”1. A US Central Command spokesperson told Al Jazeera the strait remains open, “with 95 percent of vessels getting through”1.

The print. The hormuz.now counter, which tracks ship transponder (AIS) signals, logged six commercial crossings for the complete UTC day of Thursday 22 October: five into the Gulf, one out, and one of the six a tanker2. Its pre-crisis baseline is 84.8 crossings a day2. By 14:28 UTC on Friday it had five more, two of them tankers, and its rolling seven-day average stood at 4.1 a day3. Desk arithmetic: Thursday was about 7% of a pre-war day.

The fine print in the print. The counter says plainly that its counts are “AIS-visible only and miss ships running dark”3. That matters here. Lloyd’s List Intelligence reported on Thursday that tankers willing to risk the voyage have been moving at night through a US-protected lane near Oman, with location systems and mobile phones switched off, and transferring oil to other tankers in the Gulf of Oman4. So the true figure is higher than six. Nobody outside the navies knows how much higher.

The gap. “95 percent of vessels getting through” is a share of those that try. It says nothing about how many try. “More than before the war” is a volume claim, and no public count supports it. The counter is incomplete in a known direction; the claim is complete in no direction at all.

Verdict. The podium offers a number without a ledger. The print offers a ledger with a declared blind spot. When IMF PortWatch publishes its own count for these days, you will have a second, independent ledger. Until then, a statement that more oil flows than before the war should be treated as an opening bid. Nothing here is advice.

Sources

  1. Iran says seven ships hit in Hormuz Strait, warns US of wider response — Al Jazeera (with AFP and AP)
  2. Strait of Hormuz traffic on Thursday 22 October 2026 — hormuz.now
  3. Strait of Hormuz traffic on Friday 23 October 2026 — hormuz.now
  4. Iran says seven oil tankers damaged in Strait of Hormuz in largest single-day record — SBS News (AP)

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Podium vs Print: "a promise to keep" and €5.4 billion
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Sixteen state premiers told Berlin to cut the electricity tax as fast as possible. The federal finance ministry puts the cost at about €5.4 billion a year. A promise is free to repeat; a tax cut has an invoice.
item.content:encoded:
Sixteen state premiers told Berlin to cut the electricity tax as fast as possible. The federal finance ministry puts the cost at about €5.4 billion a year. A promise is free to repeat; a tax cut has an invoice.

The podium. On Thursday the sixteen state premiers, Social Democrats included, called on the federal government “to take financial measures as quickly as possible so that a cut in the electricity tax is possible for everyone”. Their chair, Gordon Schnieder, added: “Das haben wir versprochen und das ist zu halten” — we promised that, and it must be kept1. (English quotes in this piece are the desk’s translations from German.)

The answer. On Friday the deputy government spokesman, Steffen Meyer, said the cut is in the coalition agreement and “there is the clear goal of implementing it fully in the end”. Then the clause: like every project, it stands “under a financing proviso”1. He named no date. Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil had said on Thursday, after the tax estimate, that anyone proposing a cut “should at the same time bring proposals for how to finance it”1.

The print. The electricity tax for households is 2.05 cents per kilowatt hour; the EU minimum is 0.1 cent2. A cut to the minimum for all consumers would cost about €5.4 billion a year, by the finance ministry’s estimate2. So far the cut applies only to manufacturing companies and to agriculture and forestry2.

What it would mean at home. Including VAT, the cut would save about 2.32 cents per kilowatt hour, if suppliers pass it on in full2. That is roughly €58 a year for a two-person household using 2,500 kWh, €81 for three people at 3,500 kWh and €104 for a family of four at 4,500 kWh2. Desk arithmetic: at €5.4 billion a year, every year of delay costs the federal budget nothing and costs a family of four about €104.

The gap. The Länder demand and the federal answer both say yes to the goal. Only one side holds the ledger it would come out of. Chancellor Merz has pointed to higher revenue from stronger growth; the finance ministry does not think that is enough to cover the shortfall1.

Verdict. A demand without a funding line is a podium. A cost estimate without a decision is a print waiting for a vote. The day the cut becomes real is the day someone publishes where the €5.4 billion comes from. Until then, plan with the bill you have. Nothing here is advice.

Sources

  1. Bundesregierung sagt trotz Drängens der Länder keine schnelle Stromsteuersenkung zu — Reuters via onvista
  2. Stromsteuer-Senkung: So hoch wäre die Entlastung für Verbraucher — StromAuskunft

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Britons felt worse faster than they spent less
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: GfK's consumer confidence index fell eleven points in a month, the steepest drop outside the pandemic since the Brexit vote. On the same morning the official till receipts showed volumes down just 0.4%, with fuel up. Mood moves first; wallets move slower.
item.content:encoded:
GfK's consumer confidence index fell eleven points in a month, the steepest drop outside the pandemic since the Brexit vote. On the same morning the official till receipts showed volumes down just 0.4%, with fuel up. Mood moves first; wallets move slower.

Two British numbers arrived on Friday morning, both about households, and they did not agree.

The feeling. GfK’s consumer confidence index fell eleven points to −24 in October, below every forecast in a Reuters poll1. It was the biggest month-on-month drop since April 2020, the first lockdown; outside the pandemic, the last fall on this scale came after the June 2016 Brexit vote1. GfK said no single factor explained it, pointing to rising inflation, the war in the Middle East and the squeeze on budgets. “The speed of this deterioration is alarming,” said Neil Bellamy of GfK1. The survey asked 2,003 adults between 1 and 14 October1.

The behaviour. The Office for National Statistics reported that retail sales volumes fell 0.4% in September, after a 0.7% rise in August2. Over the third quarter they rose 0.7%2. Fuel volumes rose on the month “despite fuel prices continuing to rise”, after a fall in August when retailers thought motorists were only partly filling their tanks2. Clothing fell, which online retailers put down to a warm September, the joint-fourth warmest on record2.

Why they differ. They cover different months, for a start: the ONS figures stop in September, the GfK survey ran in early October. But the gap is also a familiar one in behavioural research. People report their expectations quickly and strongly; they change their routines slowly and partly. A full tank is a habit; a gloomy answer to a pollster costs nothing.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the mood is wrong. Confidence surveys often lead spending. It means a single bad survey is a warning light, not a verdict. The ONS will publish October’s figures on 20 November2. That is the month to watch.

For you. When the news tells you everyone feels poorer, check whether anyone is actually buying less. Your own spending is the one series you can read daily. Nothing here is advice.

Sources

  1. UK consumer confidence tumbles ahead of Healey's budget, GfK reports — Reuters via Investing.com
  2. Retail sales, Great Britain: September 2026 — Office for National Statistics

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Eleven refineries and a dialogue
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Berlin opened talks with the oil industry on keeping Germany's refineries. The press release starts where a strategy should: with an inventory of eleven sites and 92 million tonnes a year. The hard part, who pays for the conversion, is still a study.
item.content:encoded:
Berlin opened talks with the oil industry on keeping Germany's refineries. The press release starts where a strategy should: with an inventory of eleven sites and 92 million tonnes a year. The hard part, who pays for the conversion, is still a study.
