The Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy opened a dialogue with the mineral oil industry on Friday about the future of Germany’s refineries1. Minister Katherina Reiche’s ministry will turn it into a strategy paper for the cabinet; the Länder, the IG BCE union and affected industries are to be brought in1,2.

The inventory. The release starts with the stock. Germany has eleven refinery sites with a processing capacity of a little over 92 million tonnes of crude a year1. They cover a large part of the fuel used on roads, in the air and at sea, and make feedstocks for plastics and medicines1. Keeping that capacity is called “a strategic priority” of industrial policy1.

The claim. The ministry argues that losing these refineries “cannot be compensated by imports” and would threaten chemical companies or push them abroad1. It also says the plants must convert step by step from fossil to sustainable feedstocks, which needs “investments in the billions”, and that companies need to be able to plan long-term and assess risks reliably1.

What is missing. The release does not say who pays for those billions, or what instruments the state might use. It announces a cross-ministry study on what a resilient energy system needs and how resilience can be anchored in planning, scenarios and administration1. That is a sensible order: count, then study, then decide. It is also slow, at a time when a war in the Gulf is setting fuel prices week by week.

Why the timing makes sense anyway. The release itself names the reason: international conflicts and attacks on energy infrastructure show how much a resilient fuel supply matters1. Gasoil, the middle distillate behind diesel and heating oil, traded at $1,486.50 a tonne on Friday afternoon3. Refineries are where crude becomes the things you actually buy.

The constructive reading. Germans tend to discover their infrastructure only when it fails. A dialogue that begins with a list of sites, capacities and products, before any plant has closed, is the dull and correct way round. Watch for the study’s terms of reference. That will tell you whether this is a strategy or a press release.

Sources

  1. Bundesregierung startet Raffineriestrategie: Resilienz stärken, Wettbewerbsfähigkeit sichern, Transformation ermöglichen — Bundesministerium für Wirtschaft und Energie (BMWE)
  2. Sicherung der Raffinerien: Bundesregierung startet Strategie — Deutschlandfunk
  3. Heizölpreise aktuell für Deutschland (gasoil quote) — HeizOel24

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: The survey cooled the committee
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Euro-area business growth slowed to a four-month low in October, France shrank, and firms raised their prices more slowly even as their energy costs rose. Six days before the ECB meets, that is the print the hawks did not want.
item.content:encoded:
Euro-area business growth slowed to a four-month low in October, France shrank, and firms raised their prices more slowly even as their energy costs rose. Six days before the ECB meets, that is the print the hawks did not want.

The S&P Global flash composite PMI for the euro area fell to 51.9 in October from 53.1 in September, its lowest since June and below every forecast in a Reuters poll, which had expected 52.71. Above 50 still means growth. Services fell to 51.7 and manufacturing to 52.43.

Where it weakened. France’s composite fell to 48.4 from 51.1, back into contraction, against 50.5 expected2. Firms there tied a sharp fall in demand to political uncertainty, and business confidence hit its lowest since 2012 outside the pandemic1. Germany kept growing, but more slowly, at 52.8 from 53.82. Hiring across the currency area almost stopped1.

The price detail. This is the line for the European Central Bank. Input costs rose faster for a second month, driven by energy, fuel and transport1. Yet firms raised their own selling prices more slowly than in September, which points to margins being squeezed rather than costs passed on1. “There is still little evidence of second-round effects, which will be reassuring for the ECB,” said Harry Chambers of Capital Economics1.

The good line. New export orders rose for a third consecutive month, after nearly four and a half years of declines1. Chris Williamson of S&P Global said the reading is consistent with growth of about 0.3% a quarter, “still among some of the best performances seen over the past three years”3.

The committee. The ECB meets on 28–29 October with its deposit rate at 2.50%. A Reuters poll earlier this month expected a hold next week and a quarter-point rise in December, with inflation running nearly double the 2% target1. Traders scaled back bets on further rises after the surveys2. Across the Atlantic, a December Fed hike is no longer fully priced either4.

What it means. An energy shock that raises costs but not prices is painful for firms and, for now, less dangerous for inflation. A central bank that waits for evidence before acting is doing its job, not dithering. Nothing here is advice.

Sources

  1. Euro zone growth slows to 4-month low amid rising costs and French strife, survey shows — Reuters via Investing.com
  2. Euro area flash PMI slips to 51.9 in October as France falls into contraction — Optencis
  3. Eurozone HCOB Composite PMI declines to 51.9 in October vs. 52.7 expected — FXStreet
  4. Tech selloff relents, oil at five-month high — Reuters via Investing.com

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Podium vs Print: "off the charts" and 6.7 per cent
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Nvidia's chief executive said demand for AI clouds is off the charts and capital is what is missing. The chip index fell 6.72% the same day. The market heard the second half of the sentence.
item.content:encoded:
Nvidia's chief executive said demand for AI clouds is off the charts and capital is what is missing. The chip index fell 6.72% the same day. The market heard the second half of the sentence.

The podium. Speaking to CNBC in Berlin on Thursday, Jensen Huang said: “If you look at the fundamentals, the demand for the neo clouds is off the charts”1. Neoclouds are the specialised firms that rent out AI computing power. He went on: “What is missing in the middle is the working capital to fuel that growth … because there’s just so much demand across so many sectors of AI, there’s a scarcity of capital”1.

The print. By the close the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index had fallen 6.72% to 10,731.982. Lam Research lost 11.76% after its results, AMD 8.1%, Nvidia 4.4% and Broadcom 4.31%2. Meta fell 7% after reporting negative free cash flow, and the Nasdaq lost 2.6%, its worst day since early June2. CoreWeave, which CNBC calls the poster child for borrowing to build data centres, dropped 10%3.

The gap. Mr Huang made two statements, and investors weighed the second. Demand that has to be financed by borrowing is demand with a credit risk attached. Dario Perkins of TS Lombard put it plainly: until recently hyperscalers invested out of cash flow, but now “debt is now the marginal source of funding”1. He expects AI companies to issue around $700 billion of new bonds in 20271. If credit markets fund the margin, he warned, someone outside the AI ecosystem can “turn off the credit taps”1.

The other side. The businesses are not failing. Meta’s revenue grew 26% in the September quarter, and FactSet expects the “Magnificent Seven” to report earnings growth of about 33%1. On Friday chip stocks such as Micron and AMD were up more than 1% in early trading3. Ed Yardeni called the trade a bubble but said “taking some air out” is “a good thing”3.

Verdict. “Off the charts” describes an order book. Minus 6.72% describes what the market thinks the order book will cost to fill. Both can be true. The dull number that settles it will not be a keynote; it will be interest rates on the next bond issue. Nothing here is advice.

Sources

  1. Emerging credit risk: What could take out the AI trade — CNBC
  2. Jensen Huang called AI demand 'off the charts,' and chip stocks still had one of their worst days of the year — Invested Alpha
  3. Stocks open lower as U.S. oil tops $100 amid escalating Iran tensions: Live updates — CNBC

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Ebola passed 9,700 confirmed cases
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: The Bundibugyo outbreak in Congo reached 9,704 confirmed cases and 4,687 deaths. Kenya has nine cases, Nigeria one with 44 contacts. Europe's disease agency keeps its risk low and its advice dull: inform travellers, do not screen arrivals.
item.content:encoded:
The Bundibugyo outbreak in Congo reached 9,704 confirmed cases and 4,687 deaths. Kenya has nine cases, Nigeria one with 44 contacts. Europe's disease agency keeps its risk low and its advice dull: inform travellers, do not screen arrivals.

As of 21 October, the Democratic Republic of the Congo had reported 9,704 confirmed cases of Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus, including 4,687 deaths, in data up to 20 October1. Since the previous update there were 67 new confirmed cases and 41 deaths, in Ituri, North Kivu and Tshopo1. 1,041 patients are in isolation, and 2,595 people who tested positive have recovered1.

Where. Ituri remains the centre, with 7,040 cases and 3,271 deaths; North Kivu has 2,146 cases1. In all, 66 of 178 health zones in eight provinces are affected1. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control says the outbreak is probably larger than reported, because of gaps in data and contact follow-up1.

Beyond Congo. Kenya has nine confirmed cases, including one death, all linked to a first case imported from Congo; 134 of 135 contacts are in quarantine1. Nigeria reported its first case on 20 October, a woman who flew in from Uganda; 44 close contacts are being monitored1. Uganda’s own outbreak was declared over in August1.

The risk for Europe. ECDC rates the likelihood of infection as low for people living in or travelling to affected areas, and very low for people living in the EU/EEA1. It also says screening returning travellers “would not be effective” in keeping the virus out, based on the 2013–2016 West African outbreak. Priority should go to giving travellers clear information on symptoms and what to do if they fall ill after arrival1.

What is missing. There is still no licensed vaccine or specific treatment for Bundibugyo virus1. WHO guidance proposes using the licensed Ervebo vaccine, made for a different Ebola species, mainly within research protocols; Congo began vaccinating frontline workers with it in August1.

The constructive reading. The numbers are grim, and they are numbers: counted, published, broken down by health zone. Kenya found 134 of 135 contacts. That is what an outbreak response looks like when it works, one list at a time.

Sources

  1. Ebola disease outbreak caused by Bundibugyo virus – Multi-country – 2026 (update of 22 October) — European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC)

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Trappes, and the seventy thousand
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: A gunman killed one person and seriously wounded several others in two towns west of Paris; anti-terror prosecutors have the case. Hours later the interior minister set out 70,000 police and gendarmes for Saturday's protests. One day, two tests of the same institutions.
item.content:encoded:
A gunman killed one person and seriously wounded several others in two towns west of Paris; anti-terror prosecutors have the case. Hours later the interior minister set out 70,000 police and gendarmes for Saturday's protests. One day, two tests of the same institutions.

At about 10:30 on Friday a man opened fire from a car in Trappes and La Verrière, two towns in the Yvelines west of Paris, killing one person and seriously wounding several others1. Among the wounded is a 12-year-old girl, now reported stable at Necker hospital in Paris1. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said one person had been killed and four injured, and that the suspect had been arrested1.

What is established. The suspect, 39, was arrested in Coignières and is in custody1. The national anti-terrorism prosecutor’s office (Pnat) has opened an investigation for murder and attempted murders “in relation with a terrorist enterprise”, with the aggravating circumstance that the acts were committed because of the victims’ real or supposed race, ethnicity, nation or religion, and for possession of a category A weapon1. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez called it “clearly a terrorist crime”1. According to franceinfo’s sources, the suspect’s flat was found booby-trapped1. His motives have not been officially stated1.

What is not. Local officials have offered readings of a possible motive; the minister declined to go beyond calling it “a murderous rampage”1. This desk will wait for the prosecutor. Speculation in the first hours of an attack has a poor record and a high cost.

Saturday. Hours later Mr Nuñez set out the security plan for Saturday’s protests against the cost of living and in support of school students: 70,000 police and gendarmes across the country, 10,000 more than on 17 October2. Raid, GIGN and BRI units will guard public buildings rather than police marches; about twenty Centaure armoured vehicles and some fifteen water cannon will be deployed2. Prefects may ban marches where safety cannot be ensured, and routes away from shopping districts are preferred2. About 2,400 people were arrested on 17 October and nearly 500 more in the following days2.

The constructive reading. France’s institutions were asked two different questions on Friday: how to respond to an attack, and how to protect the right to protest without another night like Limoges. The answer to both is the same boring set of tools: a prosecutor with a clear remit, police inquiries that are counted and published, and rules announced the day before rather than improvised on the night.

Sources

  1. Un mort et plusieurs blessés graves, un suspect arrêté, "un crime terroriste"... Ce que l'on sait de l'attaque à l'arme à feu à Trappes et La Verrière — franceinfo
  2. Blindés, unités d'élite, 70 000 policiers et gendarmes… Laurent Nuñez détaille l'important dispositif de sécurité mobilisé pour les manifestations du 24 octobre — franceinfo

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: The storm went west, the Rhine got a day
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Storm Austen cut power to 288,600 homes in north-west France with gusts of 161 km/h. In Germany, the Rhine at Kaub spent its first full day this autumn above its 2018 low. The same weather system, two very different invoices.
item.content:encoded:
Storm Austen cut power to 288,600 homes in north-west France with gusts of 161 km/h. In Germany, the Rhine at Kaub spent its first full day this autumn above its 2018 low. The same weather system, two very different invoices.

Storm Austen, the first autumn storm of the year, crossed north-west France on Friday1. By Friday midday the grid operator Enedis counted about 288,600 homes without power: 148,500 in Brittany, 88,800 in Pays de la Loire, 49,600 in Normandy and 7,800 in Hauts-de-France1. Météo-France recorded gusts of 161 km/h at the Pointe du Raz in Finistère1. Firefighters in the department had intervened 384 times since the start of the episode, and three people in Brittany suffered electric shocks1. No serious injuries had been reported by midday1.

The trains and planes. Rail traffic was halted as a precaution on Normandy’s lines and partly in Brittany and the north, with disruption expected on Saturday too; flights at Roissy, Orly and Nantes were delayed or cancelled, and DFDS cancelled Dover–Calais crossings until Saturday morning1.

The river. Several hundred kilometres east, a quieter number moved, and in the right direction. The Rhine gauge at Kaub has stayed at or above 25 cm all day on Friday, between 25 and 29 cm, for a daily mean so far of 27.3 cm by 16:152. Twenty-five centimetres was the lowest daily reading of the 2010–2020 reference decade, set on 22 October 20182,4. Desk arithmetic: the thirty daily means before Friday all sat below it, five of them below zero. Discharge stood at 547 cubic metres a second at 16:003. This morning’s edition asked whether the day would hold. By 16:15, it had.

What it is not. It is not a recovery. The gauge is still 51 cm short of the 77 cm reference at which the shipping channel depth is guaranteed, the equivalent water level GlW, with a mean water level of 208 cm4. One day above a line is a data point, not a trend.

The constructive reading. Both stories run on public measurement. Enedis counts homes off the grid by region; Météo-France publishes gusts by station; the federal waterways office publishes the Rhine every fifteen minutes, free to use1,2. Repair crews, barge operators and insurers plan on exactly these numbers. A storm is frightening. A storm that is measured is a job list.

Sources

  1. Tempête Austen : 288 600 foyers privés d'électricité, perturbations dans les aéroports et sur les rails... Le point sur les intempéries en milieu d'après-midi — franceinfo
  2. PEGELONLINE REST API: Kaub (Rhein), water level W, 15-minute raw values for the last 32 days — Wasserstraßen- und Schifffahrtsverwaltung des Bundes (WSV)
  3. PEGELONLINE REST API: Kaub station, current values (W, Q) — WSV
  4. PEGELONLINE REST API: Kaub station, characteristic values (NW, MW, GlW) — WSV

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: The market met before the committees did
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Three central banks meet next week. On Thursday a tech sell-off did some of their deliberating for them: the biggest Treasury rally since March 2023, a stronger yen, and half a hike priced out. France was the exception.
item.content:encoded:
Three central banks meet next week. On Thursday a tech sell-off did some of their deliberating for them: the biggest Treasury rally since March 2023, a stronger yen, and half a hike priced out. France was the exception.

Next week three committees sit down. The Federal Reserve meets, the European Central Bank is expected to hold its deposit rate at 2.5%, and the Bank of Japan decides on Friday4. On Thursday, before any of them had opened a briefing book, the bond market held its own meeting, and it voted for less.

The trigger was an invoice, not a speech. Meta reported negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion for the third quarter and raised the bottom of its full-year capital spending range to $135 billion, from $130 billion; the price of insuring its five-year debt reached an all-time high, CNBC reported3. Reuters called it the company’s first cash outflow in more than a decade1. The Nasdaq Composite fell 2.6%, its worst day since June, and the S&P 500 1.2%, its worst since July2.

The bond vote. Money went where it usually goes when shares fall: into US Treasuries. The 10-year yield fell more than 19 basis points overnight, the biggest drop since March 2023, before steadying at 4.9591% on Friday, back below 5%1. The 2-year yield fell nearly 19 basis points to 4.6566%1. The 2-year is the committee’s yield, the one that moves with expectations for the Fed, and it moved as much as the long one.

That is where the committee arithmetic changed. Markets “sharply pared back” expectations of further Fed tightening, stripping out almost a full quarter-point hike for next year, Reuters reported; a December rise is no longer fully priced, with the implied probability down to 85%1. ING’s analysts put it plainly: “The risk-off environment takes pressure off the Fed to hike next week”4.

The currency vote. The yen strengthened to 156.28 per dollar, its strongest in more than a month, and was set for a 1% gain on the week4. The dollar index was at 101.52, near its lowest since the start of the month, and the Swiss franc held near its firmest in a month at 0.8199 per dollar4. OCBC’s analysts, quoted by Reuters, sorted the havens by fear: AI jitters favour the yen, oil fears favour the Canadian dollar and the Norwegian crown, and French fiscal stress favours the franc4.

The exception. Not every ten-year bond was a refuge. France’s benchmark yield rose another 6 basis points overnight to 5.0601%, its highest since 2002, while Japan’s fell 9 basis points to 2.790% and Australia’s 10 basis points to 5.164%1.

Desk arithmetic: on Friday morning’s figures, France paid about 10 basis points more than the United States to borrow for ten years. The euro, at $1.122, was held back by the same worry4. A safe haven is not a nationality. It is a budget that markets believe will pass.

Tokyo’s homework. Japan handed its committee a fresh number on Friday. Core consumer prices, excluding fresh food, rose 2.1% in September from a year earlier, up from 1.7% in August; the measure that also strips out energy, which the BOJ watches closely, rose 2.4%5. Most economists polled by Reuters expect the Bank of Japan to hold next Friday and raise rates by a quarter point in December4. That is a poll, not a decision, and the desk records it as one.

What this is not. It is not a verdict on the economy. Brent settled at $113.17 on Thursday, its highest since May2, and expensive oil does not make committees relax. ING expects the 10-year yield to “snap back above (5%)” eventually, citing inflation, the deficit and the AI boom1. A single session can move a probability; it cannot write a minute.

Here is the constructive part, and it is a dull one. “US Treasury bonds are — gasp — working as your hedge again,” wrote Nomura’s Charlie McElligott1. The word that matters is “again”. On Thursday shares and bonds parted company, and the mechanism that is supposed to cushion a household’s pension when shares slide did roughly what it says on the tin. Lower long yields also lifted the shares of homebuilders and regional banks, CNBC reported2, which is how a bond rally eventually reaches a mortgage quote.

Next week the committees will read the same screens you have read here, plus the data you have not: wages, prices, order books. They do not need to agree with Thursday’s vote. They only need to explain theirs. Nothing here is advice.

Sources

  1. Asian shares wobble as tech rout boosts bonds, dents rate hike bets — Reuters via Euronext
  2. Stock futures are little changed after tech sector sell-off: Live updates — CNBC
  3. Meta stock sinks nearly 7% as AI spend pushes free cash flow negative — CNBC
  4. Yen shines as AI jitters spur safe-haven rush — Reuters via Free Malaysia Today
  5. Japan core inflation in September surges to its highest this year at 2.1% — CNBC

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Capital became the scarce input
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: The Nasdaq had its worst day since June after Meta's cash flow turned negative. The Dow closed flat, and Nvidia's chief said out loud what the bond market was pricing: money for the AI build-out is no longer unlimited.
item.content:encoded:
The Nasdaq had its worst day since June after Meta's cash flow turned negative. The Dow closed flat, and Nvidia's chief said out loud what the bond market was pricing: money for the AI build-out is no longer unlimited.

Thursday’s sell-off had a clear invoice behind it. Meta reported negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion for the third quarter and raised the floor of its full-year capital spending range to $135 billion; its shares fell almost 7% and the spread on its five-year credit default swaps reached an all-time high2. Revenue still grew 26%, to $64.60 billion, ahead of forecasts2. Investors were not doubting that Meta sells advertising. They were doubting how long it can spend faster than it earns.

The doubt spread down the supply chain. The US technology sector fell 3%; Nvidia lost 4.4%, Alphabet 3.2% and Advanced Micro Devices 8.1%1. Tesla fell 3.1% after cutting its 2026 capital spending plans3. The Nasdaq Composite fell 2.6%, its worst day since June, and the S&P 500 1.2%, its worst since July1. The Dow Jones Industrial Average, heavier in banks and industrials, closed marginally higher1.

The most useful sentence of the day came from a seller of the shovels. “There’s a scarcity of capital. The demand [for] the capital is much greater than the availability of the capital,” Nvidia’s Jensen Huang told CNBC, speaking about the smaller cloud companies of the AI build-out1. Ed Yardeni called the AI trade a “bubble” but added: “Taking some air out of the AI bubble is a good thing. I don’t think it’s going to burst and create problems for the economy”1. That is a view, not a forecast the desk endorses; it is a fair description of what a correction is for.

Asia took the baton on Friday. Japan’s Nikkei fell 1.3% and was down 5% on the week; South Korea’s KOSPI fell 1.7%, on course for a 4.3% weekly loss; an index of mainland Chinese blue chips hit its lowest since July 20253. Taiwan’s market was closed for a typhoon3. US stock futures, by contrast, were roughly flat on Thursday evening1.

The calm reading is in the weekly numbers. The S&P 500 was still heading for a slim gain on the week and the Dow for a 1.7% rise1. A market that sells the biggest spenders and keeps the rest is not panicking. It is doing the dull job it exists for: asking who pays for the build-out, and at what price. Nothing here is advice.

Sources

  1. Stock futures are little changed after tech sector sell-off: Live updates — CNBC
  2. Meta stock sinks nearly 7% as AI spend pushes free cash flow negative — CNBC
  3. Asian shares wobble as tech rout boosts bonds, dents rate hike bets — Reuters via Euronext

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: A comment period for capital
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Washington published the rulebook for American money going into Chinese, Russian, Iranian, Cuban and North Korean technology. It is not a ban on everything. It is a form, a list and a deadline, which is how serious policy usually arrives.
item.content:encoded:
Washington published the rulebook for American money going into Chinese, Russian, Iranian, Cuban and North Korean technology. It is not a ban on everything. It is a form, a list and a deadline, which is how serious policy usually arrives.

On Thursday the US Treasury published a notice of proposed rulemaking for its Outbound Investment Security Program1. It turns the COINS Act, passed with the 2026 defence authorisation, into regulations1. The idea is narrow. It is not about trade in goods. It is about American capital, and the know-how that travels with it, flowing into technologies that could help a rival’s military, surveillance or cyber capabilities1.

What it does. US persons would have to notify Treasury of some investments and would be barred from others1. Five countries are covered: China, Cuba, Iran, North Korea and Russia2. Congress named five sectors: semiconductors and microelectronics, AI systems, quantum, high-performance computing and hypersonics. Treasury has added a sixth, biotechnology1. In AI, covered investments in those countries would be banned outright2. Treasury’s reason is candid: after two years of rapid progress, it doubts anyone can reliably “distinguish the most advanced models”2.

What it does not do. It does not ban all investment in those countries2. Investments in publicly traded companies are excepted, as are deals worth less than $50,000. Investors can also ask for exemptions in the US national interest2. Licensing deals by US drugmakers with China are not included, a Treasury official said, which meets a key request from the industry2. One name has left the list: Venezuela. Treasury says Maduro’s government “no longer exists”2.

Why it matters to you. If your pension fund, or a fund you hold, invests in private Chinese tech, the change shows up as compliance work long before anything is sold. Investors must make a “reasonable and diligent inquiry” before a deal, and the rule sets penalties for violations1. Assistant Secretary Chris Pilkerton put it this way: “It’s not just about the money. It’s about the network, the supply chain”2. Nothing here is advice.

The dull part, which is the good part. Comments are open until 7 December2. Only the final rule will set an effective date1. That is slower than a tweet and much harder to reverse. In a year of waivers announced from podiums, a rule with a docket, a deadline and a definitions section counts as stability.

Sources

  1. Treasury Issues Proposed Rule to Implement Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act — U.S. Department of the Treasury
  2. US Treasury drops Venezuela from countries facing outbound US investment restrictions — Reuters via Investing.com

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Podium vs Print: "they love it" and 34 per cent
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Asked how Americans feel about the Iran war, the president said that in one way they love it. The most recent Reuters/Ipsos panel, interviewed three days earlier, found a third approving of the strikes. He did leave himself a second sentence.
item.content:encoded:
Asked how Americans feel about the Iran war, the president said that in one way they love it. The most recent Reuters/Ipsos panel, interviewed three days earlier, found a third approving of the strikes. He did leave himself a second sentence.

The podium. On Thursday at the White House, Donald Trump was asked about public reaction to the Iran war. “Well, in one way they love it because I’m doing what should have been done by other presidents,” he said. “And in another way maybe they don’t.” He called the conflict “a price to pay” to stop Iran getting a nuclear weapon: “we can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon”1.

The print. The latest Reuters/Ipsos survey interviewed 1,679 US adults from 16 to 19 October, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.4 points2. Asked whether they approve of US military strikes against Iran, 34% said yes and 61% said no2. Weighing costs and benefits, 23% said the action has been worth it and 54% said it has not2. A quarter, 25%, approve of the president’s handling of Iran. Just 16% think the administration has a clear strategy, against 58% who think it does not2. And 78% expect US involvement to go on “for an extended period”, against 16% who expect it to end within weeks2.

The gap. The quote contains its own correction. “In one way… in another way maybe they don’t” is a two-sided sentence, and the panel shows which side is bigger. The love is real, but it is partisan. Among Republicans, 74% approve of the strikes; among independents, 24%; among Democrats, 11%2. Desk arithmetic: disapproval outweighs approval by 27 points overall, so “they” in the first half of the sentence describes roughly one American in three. The president is not inventing a mood. He is quoting his own room.

Verdict. The podium was half right and said so itself. The print gives the proportions: a third approve, three in five do not, and very few see a plan. None of that settles whether the war is right; polls measure consent, not wisdom. It does settle the word “love”. A democracy gets to check a president’s sense of the room with a random sample, published with its margin of error and every question in full2. That dull PDF is one of the better things about the system, and it will be read closely in the weeks before the November midterms3.

Sources

  1. Trump says US could go further in Iran war, Tehran threatens wider response (live) — Iran International
  2. Reuters/Ipsos mid-October Survey Topline — Ipsos
  3. Democrats plan to investigate U.S. diesel companies involved in easing Russian sanctions — The Washington Post

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: The child sets the rules too
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Two large family studies find that a child's aggression predicts less consistent discipline later, not the other way round. It is a finding that lifts some blame and asks for better help.
item.content:encoded:
Two large family studies find that a child's aggression predicts less consistent discipline later, not the other way round. It is a finding that lifts some blame and asks for better help.

The usual story about difficult children runs one way. Parents who enforce rules unevenly get children who hit, defy and shout. A study published in Nature Communications, led by Joanna K. Bright of King’s College London, tested that story against two large, genetically informative samples, and the arrow mostly pointed the other way1.

The two samples. The first is Norway’s Mother, Father and Child Cohort, with extended-family data on 53,532 children born to 42,538 mothers, assessed at age five1. The second is the US Early Growth and Development Study: 561 adoption triads of an adopted child, the adoptive parents and the birth parents, followed from 4.5 to 8 years1. Adoptive parents share no genes with the child, which lets you see the family environment without inheritance getting in the way1.

What they found. In Norway, about 47% of the modest link between inconsistent discipline and aggression came from shared genes; the rest pointed from child to mother, with no significant path from discipline to aggression1. The adoption study agreed: a child’s aggression predicted more inconsistent discipline at later ages, while mothers’ discipline did not significantly predict later aggression1. The authors write that “childhood aggression drives inconsistent parenting beyond shared genetic influences”1. The link between warm, positive parenting and lower aggression was, in Norway, fully explained by shared genes1.

The caveats. The measures were narrow and mostly mothers’ reports; the families were relatively advantaged; the data are 10 to 23 years old1. With fathers’ own reports, the influence ran both ways at the same age1. And when one parent rated the child and the other rated the parenting, the links vanished, which hints that one person reporting both inflates them1.

The constructive reading. None of this says parenting does not matter. It says a parent worn down by a child who pushes back is not simply the author of the pushing. The authors suggest that programmes that only coach consistent discipline “may be insufficient”1. Help that works with the child’s behaviour as well as the parent’s is a less tidy message, and probably a kinder one. Nothing here is advice.

Sources

  1. Kids' aggression appears to shape parents' discipline more than the reverse, study finds — PsyPost

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: The wind did what the Strait could not
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Brent settled at its highest since May on Thursday. The same day, German turbines nearly tripled their output, gas plants burned half as much as on Wednesday, and Friday's power cleared at €137.59.
item.content:encoded:
Brent settled at its highest since May on Thursday. The same day, German turbines nearly tripled their output, gas plants burned half as much as on Wednesday, and Friday's power cleared at €137.59.

On Thursday Brent crude jumped 4% to settle at $113.17 a barrel, its highest settlement since May, after a report that the US and Israel were drawing up plans for renewed attacks on Iran2. On Friday morning in Asia it barely moved, at $112.963. That is the headline. The German grid wrote a different one.

Onshore wind turbines in Germany generated 673.1 gigawatt hours on Thursday 22 October, up from 242.3 GWh on Wednesday, according to the Bundesnetzagentur’s SMARD data1. It was the third-best wind day since the start of September. Gas-fired plants, which on Wednesday had burned their way to 241.4 GWh, the highest of the autumn so far, fell to 123.3 GWh1. Desk arithmetic: wind up about 2.8 times, gas down by about half, in one day.

The auction followed the turbines. The day-ahead price for the Germany-Luxembourg zone, which had averaged €211.94 per megawatt hour for Wednesday’s delivery, cleared at €148.61 for Thursday and €137.59 for Friday1. Desk arithmetic: Friday’s power is about 35% cheaper than Wednesday’s, in a week when oil rose.

Do not over-read it. The October average is still €167.60 per megawatt hour over 1 to 23 October, against €94.97 over the same days of 20251. Gas still sets the price in many hours, and the wind already eased overnight: by 03:00 on Friday onshore output was running at about 19 GWh an hour, against a Thursday average of 281. A windy day does not end an energy shock. It just shows you where the exit is.

That exit is built from paperwork: planning permits, grid connections, auction rounds, transmission lines finished on time. None of it trends. All of it showed up in Thursday’s numbers, on a day when a report of strike plans moved oil by 4% and a weather front moved German power the other way. Nothing here is advice.

Sources

  1. Market data: realised generation (wind onshore, natural gas) and day-ahead price DE-LU, daily and hourly — Bundesnetzagentur / SMARD.de
  2. Stock futures are little changed after tech sector sell-off: Live updates — CNBC
  3. Oil little changed as supply concern lingers amid Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia — Reuters via Euronext

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Ordinary Ledger: the cheapest tariff climbed, the default still costs more
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: The cheapest new-customer electricity tariffs in Germany rose about ten per cent in a month, to 30.64 cents a kilowatt hour. Basic supply still sits almost ten cents above them.
item.content:encoded:
The cheapest new-customer electricity tariffs in Germany rose about ten per cent in a month, to 30.64 cents a kilowatt hour. Basic supply still sits almost ten cents above them.

The comparison portal StromAuskunft evaluates tariffs in more than 6,300 German towns every day. On Thursday its average for the cheapest new-customer electricity tariffs reached 30.64 cents a kilowatt hour, up just over ten per cent on the month and 13.6% on the year, Berliner Zeitung reported1.

The curve. The year started cheap. In January the figure was 23.84 cents, in February 23.90, helped by €6.5 billion of federal subsidy for the transmission grid charges1. It touched 27.24 cents in April, fell back to 23.47 in June, then climbed: 27.03 in August, 27.78 in September, 30.64 now1. The reason given is procurement costs: the Iran war and the Hormuz blockade pushed the European gas price at times to €59 a megawatt hour, and gas plants often set the power price1.

The default. Basic supply, the tariff you are on if you never chose one, averages 40.39 cents, almost ten cents more1. At 3,500 kilowatt hours a year that is about €1,414 against €1,072 in the cheapest tariff, a gap of roughly €3411. In Thuringia, basic supply averages 51.73 cents against 30.26 for the cheapest offer, more than €751 a year apart1. Existing customers paid 31.4 cents on average in August, according to Verivox data cited in the report1.

The geography. The cheapest town in the sample is Ringelai in Bavaria at 26.39 cents; the dearest is Lindau on Lake Constance at 40.66 cents1. Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Brandenburg and Bavaria are cheapest; Hamburg, North Rhine-Westphalia and Saarland dearest, mostly because of regional grid charges and competition1. Green tariffs cost only 0.54 cents more, about €19 a year at 3,500 kWh1.

The constructive reading. Desk arithmetic: at 3,500 kWh, January’s cheapest tariff cost €834 a year and today’s €1,072, about €238 more. That is the market. The €341 between basic supply and the cheapest offer is not the market; it is paperwork, and paperwork is the part you control. Note that new-customer prices move daily, and a contract signed today fixes today’s figure, not January’s. Nothing here is advice.

Sources

  1. Stromkosten steigen um 10 Prozent in einem Monat – doch ein Wechsel spart im Schnitt 341 Euro — Berliner Zeitung

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: The Annex: Western Digital priced the exabyte
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Revenue up 55%, and most of the extra dollars fell straight through to operating profit. The release says why in four words: exabyte growth, improved pricing.
item.content:encoded:
Revenue up 55%, and most of the extra dollars fell straight through to operating profit. The release says why in four words: exabyte growth, improved pricing.

The document. Western Digital, which makes the hard drives that fill cloud and AI data centres, published its fiscal first-quarter results on Thursday evening, for the three months to 2 October1. It is a short release with two tables, an outlook box and a dividend line. Read slowly, it is a lesson in what scarcity does to a manufacturer’s accounts.

The headline. Revenue was $4.38bn, up 55% on a year earlier and 17% on the quarter1. Non-GAAP earnings per share were $4.64, up 161%1. FactSet’s consensus had been $4.14bn and $4.11 a share, SquawkNews reported2. Chief financial officer Kris Sennesael named the cause plainly: “robust exabyte growth and improved pricing”1. More storage sold, at better prices.

The margin line. GAAP gross margin rose to 57.8% from 43.5% a year earlier; operating margin to 46.7% from 28.1%1. Desk arithmetic on the non-GAAP table: revenue rose by $1,563m year on year, operating income by $1,297m. About 83 cents of every extra dollar of sales reached operating profit. That is not what volume alone does. It is what price does when the factories already exist.

The line that fell. GAAP diluted earnings per share fell 44% on the quarter, to $4.63 from $8.211. That is not a bad quarter. Last quarter’s GAAP net income of $3.20bn sat $1.81bn above its non-GAAP figure of $1.38bn, Desk arithmetic on the release’s own table; this quarter the two are the same, $1.78bn1. A one-off flattered the comparison base. The release prints both columns side by side, which is how it should be done.

The cash. Operating cash flow was $1.60bn and free cash flow $1.38bn1. The board raised the quarterly dividend 17%, to $0.175 a share, payable on 17 December1.

The outlook. WD guides fiscal second-quarter revenue to $5.1bn, plus or minus $100m, which it says is 66% to 72% above a year earlier, with a non-GAAP gross margin of 60–61%1. Guidance is the company’s, not ours.

The constructive reading. The AI story usually gets told through chips. This release tells it through the boring part: somewhere the data has to be kept, and the people who make the drives are, for now, being paid properly for them. Nothing here is advice; it is a reading of a company’s own release.

Sources

  1. WD Reports Fiscal First Quarter 2027 Financial Results — Western Digital
  2. Western Digital Reports Higher Fiscal First-Quarter Profit and Revenue — SquawkNews

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: The shield wears off at six months
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: A study at IDWeek finds most US babies have lost detectable measles antibodies from their mothers by six months, half a year before the routine first dose. Public health labs, meanwhile, are asking for a faster test.
item.content:encoded:
A study at IDWeek finds most US babies have lost detectable measles antibodies from their mothers by six months, half a year before the routine first dose. Public health labs, meanwhile, are asking for a faster test.

A baby is born with its mother’s antibodies, and for decades that borrowed protection was one reason the first measles shot waits until 12 to 15 months in the United States1. A study presented this week at IDWeek in Washington suggests the loan runs out much sooner1.

The numbers. C. Buddy Creech of Vanderbilt and colleagues used leftover samples from 92 mother-infant pairs1. At birth, 96.7% of infants had detectable neutralising antibodies against the vaccine strain; at two months, 89.1%; at six months, 8.7%1. Against two common wild strains, B3 and D8, the six-month figures were 19.6% and 17.4%1. Antibody concentrations against the vaccine strain fell from 1,173 to 65 mIU/mL over the six months1.

Why now. The schedule was set when many mothers had immunity from infection, which passes more antibody to the baby1. Most mothers today are vaccinated and pass on less1. That matters more in a year like this one: the CDC counted 4,410 confirmed US cases by 15 October, and Pennsylvania alone 1,310 cases and five deaths in August and September1. “If measles elimination is not going to be our norm anymore, then we’re going to have to think about what the earliest reasonable time to vaccinate is,” Creech said1.

The lab bench. Health officials in California, Oregon, Washington and Hawaii have asked CDC director Erica Schwartz to validate a rapid, high-volume measles test; a request from May was denied after two months, citing “other competing priorities”2. Labs now rely on individual PCR runs, while platforms bought in the Covid years can process up to 500 tests in eight hours2. An HHS spokesperson said the agency was “prioritizing emerging technologies”2. A vaccine given within 72 hours of exposure can prevent infection, which is why speed of diagnosis is not a technicality2.

The constructive reading. Both stories point to fixable machinery. A schedule can be revised on evidence; infants from six months can already be vaccinated when travelling or in outbreak areas1. A validated protocol, once published, can be run by any lab2. Nothing here is medical advice; the schedule is a question for your paediatrician.

Sources

  1. Study: Babies lose most measles antibodies by age 6 months — Healio
  2. CDC denies approval for high-volume measles test, citing 'other priorities' — The Guardian

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Airports, pipelines and interceptors
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Overnight both capitals talked about going further. Tehran named airports and pipelines; Washington said it 'may do it a little bit further'. The number that limits both is not in any speech: how many interceptors are left on the shelf.
item.content:encoded:
Overnight both capitals talked about going further. Tehran named airports and pipelines; Washington said it 'may do it a little bit further'. The number that limits both is not in any speech: how many interceptors are left on the shelf.

Late on Thursday, Washington time, Donald Trump said at the White House that the US had “knocked the hell out of them, and we may do it a little bit further”1. A few hours later the Wall Street Journal reported Tehran’s answer, given in public and through private channels. If the US and Israel resume their air campaign, Iran would widen its strikes to airports, pipelines and other civilian and economic targets in neighbouring Gulf states1. The warnings, the paper said, are meant to deter1.

The ledger so far. The warning is believable because of what has already happened. According to the WSJ report, in the war’s first phase Iran hit US bases, embassies and the Fifth Fleet headquarters in Bahrain. It struck energy and industrial sites in the UAE, a major gas plant in Qatar and airports in Dubai, Kuwait and Bahrain1. At sea, the IMO counts 120 confirmed incidents and 24 seafarer deaths as of 22 October2. October already holds the record month, with 27 attacks on commercial ships3. On Thursday night the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted a Houthi ballistic missile fired at Riyadh1.

The binding constraint. The most useful line in the report is not a threat. It is about stock. US and Arab militaries face declining stocks of air-defence interceptors, the Journal reported, and Israel’s supplies are also under pressure. Meanwhile Iran is believed to have resumed limited ballistic-missile production from stockpiled parts1. Every threat in this war is ultimately backed by an inventory, and shelves run down before rhetoric does.

What else is moving. Not everything points up. Iraq told Riyadh it would not let its territory be used for attacks on the kingdom1. On Friday, Turkey hosts foreign ministers from Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Pakistan, Britain, France and Germany for security talks that include Hormuz1. Neither will stop a missile. Both are the kind of slow, procedural work that makes the next missile less likely.

For you. Read Iran’s list and Trump’s “a little bit further” as bargaining positions stated in public, not as timetables. The figures worth following are the IMO’s confirmed count2 and any hard number on interceptors. Speeches do not change those figures. Events do.

Sources

  1. Trump says US could go further in Iran war, Tehran threatens wider response (live) — Iran International (citing the Wall Street Journal and Reuters)
  2. Middle East - Highlighted (Confirmed) incidents — International Maritime Organization

item.title: Kaub climbed back over the 2018 line
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: For a month every daily mean at the Rhine's bottleneck sat below the low of its reference decade. At 23:45 on Thursday the gauge read 26 cm. By 05:00 it read 28.
item.content:encoded:
For a month every daily mean at the Rhine's bottleneck sat below the low of its reference decade. At 23:45 on Thursday the gauge read 26 cm. By 05:00 it read 28.

Yesterday this desk reported that the Rhine gauge at Kaub had spent a month below 25 cm, the lowest daily reading of its 2010–2020 reference period, set on 22 October 20182. Overnight the line was crossed. At 23:45 on Thursday the gauge read 26 cm, its first reading at or above 25 cm in the 32 days of data the federal waterways administration publishes1. At 05:00 on Friday it read 28 cm1.

The arithmetic. Desk arithmetic on the 15-minute readings: Thursday’s full daily mean came to 19.1 cm, still below the 2018 line, as every daily mean since at least 22 September has been1. Friday’s mean from midnight to 05:00 is 26.3 cm1. That is five hours, not a day, and the readings are raw data that can still be revised1. Discharge at Kaub was 555 cubic metres a second at 04:45, against 509 at 16:00 on Thursday2.

Upstream. The rise is not a local blip. At Mainz the gauge read 106 cm at 05:15 on Wednesday and 125 cm at 05:00 on Friday; at Maxau, near Karlsruhe, 295 cm and 306 cm3. Water at Kaub is water that passed those gauges first.

What it is not. 28 cm is still 180 cm below Kaub’s long-run mean of 208 cm, and 49 cm short of the 77 cm equivalent water level at which the shipping channel is guaranteed to be 1.90 m deep2. Desk arithmetic. Barges still load light. A low that has stopped getting worse is not the same as a river that works.

The constructive reading. The turn was visible to anyone at 23:45, the moment it happened, on a free public feed1. Shippers do not need a press release to know when to load an extra few hundred tonnes; they need the next quarter-hour. That is what the gauge gives them, and this morning it gave them a better number than any of the last thirty days.

Sources

  1. PEGELONLINE REST API: Kaub (Rhein), water level W, 15-minute raw values for the last 32 days — Wasserstraßen- und Schifffahrtsverwaltung des Bundes (WSV)
  2. PEGELONLINE REST API: Kaub station, current values and characteristic values (NW, MW, TuGLW) — WSV
  3. PEGELONLINE REST API: Mainz and Maxau (Rhein), water level W, 15-minute raw values for the last 2 days — WSV

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Germany burned less gas for power and paid more for it
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Brent hit a five-month high while the Gulf's barrels kept moving. German power plants burned a sixth less gas this October, and power still cost about 80% more than a year ago.
item.content:encoded:
Brent hit a five-month high while the Gulf's barrels kept moving. German power plants burned a sixth less gas this October, and power still cost about 80% more than a year ago.

Brent crude futures rose $3.19, or 2.9%, to $112.01 a barrel by 13:11 GMT on Thursday, after touching $112.68, the highest since 18 May, Reuters reported1. The triggers were the ones you have read about all week: more Houthi strikes in Saudi Arabia, and Iran’s Revolutionary Guard saying four vessels in the northern Gulf were hit and set on fire and three more struck mines west of the Strait of Hormuz1,2. On Thursday, six people told Reuters, Saudi Aramco told staff to leave its Dhahran headquarters and work from home1.

Here is the part the headline leaves out. The barrels are moving. Kpler data show oil exports from the Persian Gulf above their pre-war levels, the Guardian reported, partly because more crude now travels overland by pipeline to the Red Sea and the Gulf of Oman2. Morgan Stanley put Middle East crude exports at about 17 million barrels a day last week1. “Reports of Middle East crude oil exports exceeding pre-conflict levels are more than countered by attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz and the Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia,” said Tamas Varga of PVM Oil1.

So Thursday’s price is not a count of missing oil. It is the price of the chance that oil goes missing: insurance, rerouting, a mine field, an office tower emptied as a precaution. Nobody can invoice a probability, but everyone pays for one.

How the fear reaches you. For a household in Germany the barrel is mostly a petrol-pump and heating-oil story. The bigger bill runs through gas, and through power stations that burn it. Dutch TTF gas, Europe’s benchmark, settled at €87.43 per megawatt hour on Wednesday, up 2.78% on the day, after a rally of about 19% in October3. EU gas storage is 74.58% full, 16.0 points below the five-year average of 90.6% for the date, and has started to draw down3. Germany’s stores are 61.1% full3. The cold has arrived where the stores are thinnest: Munich 3.6°C, Berlin 5.6°C in GasRadar’s morning readings3.

The print. Now the part that sounds backwards. Germany has burned less gas for electricity this October, not more. Gas plants generated about 3,421 gigawatt hours over 1 to 21 October 2026, against about 4,054 GWh over the same days of 2025, according to the Bundesnetzagentur’s SMARD data4. Desk arithmetic: about 16% less. Solar panels made up much of the difference; their output over the same days is up by about two-fifths4. Lignite is up too4.

And yet the day-ahead auction for the Germany-Luxembourg zone averaged €169.93 per megawatt hour over 1 to 21 October, against €94.14 a year earlier4. Desk arithmetic: about 80% higher, on a sixth less gas.

The reason is the dullest rule in the market. In most hours the price is set by the last plant needed to meet demand, and in Germany that is still often a gas plant. Fewer gas hours lower your exposure; they do not lower the price of the hours that remain. When the molecule costs more, so does the marginal hour, however few of those hours there are.

You can watch the rule work day by day. Wednesday 21 October was the biggest gas-burning day since 25 February, at about 241 GWh, and it was also the dearest delivery day of the week, at €211.944. Thursday cleared at €148.61, and Friday, auctioned at midday on Thursday, at €137.594. Gas burn for those days is not yet published.

What this argues for. Not panic, and not a speech. The two lines on these charts point at the same unglamorous fixes. Every gas hour replaced by a solar or wind hour is an hour the Gulf cannot price. Every interconnector lets a windy hour in the north cover a cold hour in the south. And every percentage point in a storage cavern is a cold February that does not have to be bought on the spot market. None of this makes the news like a tanker on fire. All of it decides the invoice.

The oil market will keep reacting to words and drones. PVM’s Varga expects no de-escalation before the US midterm elections1; that is a view, not a fact, and the desk records it as such. What is a fact is the arithmetic of the last three weeks: less gas burned, more paid for each megawatt hour. A country cannot control the Strait of Hormuz. It can control how many of its hours depend on it. Nothing here is advice.

Sources

  1. Brent hits five-month high on escalating Middle East conflict — Reuters (via Yahoo Finance)
  2. Oil prices jump to five-month high as attacks threaten global supply — The Guardian
  3. European gas briefing, 22 Oct 2026: TTF 87.43 EUR/MWh, EU storage 74.6 % — GasRadar (GIE AGSI+, ICE Endex data)
  4. Market data: realised generation by source (natural gas, lignite, solar) and day-ahead price DE-LU, daily — Bundesnetzagentur / SMARD.de

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Paris paid more than Washington for ten years of money
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: On Thursday the US 10-year yield fell towards 5% while France's rose through it. Stocks fell on both sides of the Atlantic, and the bond market sorted borrowers by their budgets.
item.content:encoded:
On Thursday the US 10-year yield fell towards 5% while France's rose through it. Stocks fell on both sides of the Atlantic, and the bond market sorted borrowers by their budgets.

Thursday produced a small inversion of the usual order. France’s 10-year government bond yield rose 11.5 basis points to 5.11%, after touching 5.1415%, its highest since July 20021. The US 10-year Treasury yield went the other way, down more than 11 basis points to 5.032%, as investors bought bonds for safety2. Desk arithmetic: on those two snapshots, taken a few hours apart, Paris was paying about eight basis points more than Washington to borrow for ten years. Germany paid 3.38%1.

The reasons were different on each side. In the US, yields fell with stocks: the Nasdaq was down 1.4% and the S&P 500 0.7% in the morning, as chip stocks sold off again and investors weighed Meta’s and Tesla’s spending plans4. In France, the yield rose for reasons Reuters lists plainly: worries about repairing the public finances, street protests, and Paris’s difficulty passing a budget1. Investing.com adds the number behind the worry, a deficit of 5.4% of GDP3.

Equities did not like either story. The STOXX 600 was down 0.7% in the afternoon, the CAC 40 1% and Italy’s FTSE MIB 1.7%3. Brent crude rose 2.7% to $111.79 a barrel by midday after reports that the US is preparing renewed strikes on Iran and a Houthi drone attack on Saudi Aramco’s Shaybah field5. The cushions were dull ones: Nestlé rose after its organic sales beat expectations, and SAP gained 1.7% after its results3.

The constructive reading is not that France is in a crisis; Reuters quotes Citi’s Giada Giani noting a consensus that European institutions “are stronger today than they were 15 years ago”1. It is that the bond market has stopped grading France on the euro area’s curve and started grading it on its own. That is slower and more boring than a panic, and it is fixed by the same slow, boring thing: a budget that passes. Nothing here is advice.

Sources

  1. French debt risk premium reaches euro zone sovereign crisis levels — Reuters via Investing.com
  2. Treasury yields fall as investors weigh Middle East tensions and assess fresh jobs data — CNBC
  3. European stocks buckle under French yields, mixed tech earnings — Investing.com
  4. Stock market today: Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq tumble as oil climbs, investors weigh Tesla, Meta earnings — Yahoo Finance
  5. Europe midday: Stocks slump as oil rises; Hermes slides on results — Sharecast News

item.title: Podium vs Print: "fairly soon" and four ships
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: The US president says the Iran war will end very soon, one way or the other. By mid-afternoon on Thursday the Strait of Hormuz had seen four visible commercial crossings. Soon is a word; four is a count.
item.content:encoded:
The US president says the Iran war will end very soon, one way or the other. By mid-afternoon on Thursday the Strait of Hormuz had seen four visible commercial crossings. Soon is a word; four is a count.

The podium. Flying back from a rally in South Carolina, President Trump told reporters: “No, I think we’re not negotiating.” Then: “We are going to have something one way or the other that’ll happen fairly soon”1. At the rally itself he said: “It’ll end very soon. We could leave now, but we want to make sure it lasts for a long time”1. He added that “most people seem to think it’s after the election”1. That puts the timing after the 3 November midterms, without saying what “it” is.

The print. The waterway keeps its own minutes. By 14:25 UTC on Thursday, the hormuz.now counter had logged four AIS-visible commercial crossings of the Strait of Hormuz: three into the Gulf and one out2. One was a tanker, the 182-metre Yoko 1, bound for Iraq; the other three were a container ship and two bulk carriers2. The seven-day average is 3.1 crossings a day, against a pre-crisis baseline of 84.82. Desk arithmetic: that average is under 4% of a normal day. Wednesday’s full day closed at ten.

The noise between them. Overnight, Iranian state television said four vessels involved in oil transfers in the northern Gulf had been struck and set on fire, and three more had hit mines west of the strait3. The Associated Press could not confirm the claims, and the British monitor UKMTO had not reported them3. UKMTO does say October has had the most reported attacks on shipping since March, and it notes that some shippers are now reluctant to report incidents3. The Revolutionary Guards again threatened US bases if Washington keeps guiding ships through3.

The gap. “Fairly soon” has no date and no object. It could mean a deal or more bombing, and its own speaker says it may come after a vote1. The counter has a date, a time and a list of ships with names and flags2. Neither tells you the future. Only one of them can be checked tomorrow morning.

Verdict. The podium promises an ending. The print shows a strait running at a few per cent of normal, on a day when Iran claims seven ships were hit. If you want to know when “soon” arrives, don’t listen for an announcement. Watch for the daily count to rise for a week in a row. Nothing here is advice.

Sources

  1. Trump says US 'not negotiating' with Iran, something will happen 'fairly soon' — Anadolu Agency
  2. Strait of Hormuz traffic on Thursday 22 October 2026 — hormuz.now
  3. Iran says 7 ships have been struck in Strait of Hormuz, Saudis intercept drones in airspace — CBC News (The Associated Press, with files from Reuters)

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Podium vs Print: the one per cent met the debt brake
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Ten days ago the chancellor said one point of extra growth gives the room to cut the electricity tax for everyone. Today's tax estimate found the growth, and the finance ministry found no room. Both are telling the truth about different lines.
item.content:encoded:
Ten days ago the chancellor said one point of extra growth gives the room to cut the electricity tax for everyone. Today's tax estimate found the growth, and the finance ministry found no room. Both are telling the truth about different lines.

The podium. On 12 October Friedrich Merz announced that the electricity tax should fall “for everyone” to the European minimum, households included, using “financial room in the budget” that could appear “if growth firms up”1. His arithmetic was simple: one point of growth is worth about €10 billion in extra tax in Germany, half of it for the federal government. “Das ist genau das eine Prozent Wachstum, was uns diese Spielräume gibt”, he said: that is exactly the one per cent that gives us this room1.

The print. On Thursday the tax estimators delivered the growth part. The government’s autumn projection now has 1.3% for this year and 1.1% for next, up from 0.5% and 0.9%3. Revenue for all levels of government in 2027 is €10.9 billion above the May estimate; for the years to 2030 the plus is €43.4 billion3. The federal share for 2027 is €4.1 billion3. Then the ministry’s own headline: “insgesamt keine Spielräume in 2027”, no room overall2. Lars Klingbeil put it this way: “we gain no new room, but we do not have to close new gaps either”2. The extra money flows mainly to the Länder and municipalities; at federal level, some years come in below May2.

The gap. Two things sit between the podium and the print. The first is the debt brake’s cyclical component: the better the economy runs, the less the federal government may borrow, so much of the tax plus is expected to be “eaten up” by a lower borrowing limit3. The second is the bill. Cutting the electricity tax to the EU minimum for households and small firms is expected to cost about €5.4 billion a year, and the CDU/CSU’s other wish, offsetting cold progression, about €4 billion next year3. Desk arithmetic: the two together are about €9.4 billion, more than twice the federal plus, before the debt brake takes its share. For a household, the tax cut is real money: from 2.05 to 0.1 cents per kWh1, so about €68 a year on 3,500 kWh, or about €81 with 19% VAT (desk arithmetic).

Verdict. Merz was right that growth produces tax, and the estimate confirms it. He skipped the line in the constitution that converts good times into smaller deficits. That is not a scandal; it is the rule doing what it was written to do. The useful fight now is the dull one in the Budget Committee in mid-November: which levy, which saving, which line pays for the cut3. Until someone names it, the promise is a podium and the €4.1 billion is the print. Nothing here is advice.

Sources

  1. CDU will Stromsteuer „für alle“ auf EU-Minimum absenken: Merz sieht „Spielräume“ — stern.de (AFP)
  2. Stabile Entwicklung 2026, insgesamt keine Spielräume in 2027 und weiterhin Konsolidierungsbedarf (Ergebnisse der 171. Steuerschätzung) — Bundesministerium der Finanzen
  3. ROUNDUP: Steuereinnahmen ziehen an - Klingbeil: keine Etat-Entlastung — dpa-AFX via onvista

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: More young adults feel it, not more of it
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: A US survey study finds daily anxiety among 18- to 25-year-olds rose from 15% to 19.5% between 2020 and 2024, while its reported intensity did not. The rise is in how many, and in who gets a name for it.
item.content:encoded:
A US survey study finds daily anxiety among 18- to 25-year-olds rose from 15% to 19.5% between 2020 and 2024, while its reported intensity did not. The rise is in how many, and in who gets a name for it.

A study published in the American Journal of Public Health looked at nearly 11,000 Americans aged 18 to 25 who answered the National Health Interview Survey between 2020 and 20241. Its headline is plain: nearly one in five said they felt anxious every day in 2024, up from 15% in 20201.

The three lines. The rise shows up everywhere you would look for it. Daily anxiety went from 15% to 19.5%; a reported anxiety diagnosis from 17.9% to 23.4%; prescription anxiety medication from 9.8% to 13.3%1. Desk arithmetic: each moved by roughly 30-36% in four years.

The line that did not move. The intensity respondents reported “didn’t change significantly overall”1. That is the quiet finding. More young adults are anxious every day, but the typical anxious young adult does not describe it as worse than in 2020. A society can respond to “more people” with capacity, and to “worse” with urgency; this survey points at the first.

Who, not just how many. The authors, led by Melissa Villodas of George Mason University, looked at groups in combination rather than one at a time1. In 2024, 44.6% of lesbian, gay and bisexual respondents reported a diagnosis, against 18.5% of straight respondents, and their medication use doubled from 12.9% to 26%1. Among women, 32.1% reported a diagnosis, against 14.7% of men1. And 31.3% of white respondents reported a diagnosis, against 12.7% of Black and 15.3% of Hispanic respondents, although Black and white young adults did not differ significantly in reported intensity1. The researchers point to access to care, stigma and how symptoms are recognised1.

The constructive reading. The study cannot say what caused the rise after 20201. What it can do is tell a health system where to look: at groups whose anxiety is as strong but less often diagnosed. A survey that repeats every year, asks the same questions and gets published is unglamorous machinery. It is also how you find out that a gap is in the clinic door rather than in the person. Nothing here is medical advice.

Sources

  1. Study finds 1 in 5 young adults in the U.S. experience daily anxiety — George Mason University via Medical Xpress

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Podium vs Print: "no fragmentation", and the widest French spread since 2011
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Six days ago the Banque de France governor said the conditions for ECB help were not met. On Thursday France paid 173.58 basis points over Germany, and every other spread widened with it. He may still be right; the test he set is the one to watch.
item.content:encoded:
Six days ago the Banque de France governor said the conditions for ECB help were not met. On Thursday France paid 173.58 basis points over Germany, and every other spread widened with it. He may still be right; the test he set is the one to watch.

The podium. On 16 October Emmanuel Moulin, governor of the Banque de France, told AFP that the ECB has instruments “when disorderly and unjustified market movements can disrupt the transmission of monetary policy”, but that “today, those conditions are not met. We are not seeing financial fragmentation in the euro area”1. He blamed the rise in French borrowing costs mainly on “uncertainties over the budget vote”, said banks and insurers could cope, and prescribed “fiscal consolidation” rather than central bank action1.

The print. On Thursday morning France’s 10-year yield rose 11.5 basis points to 5.11%, after touching 5.1415%, its highest since July 20022. The premium over German Bunds reached 173.58 basis points, the widest since November 2011, in the euro debt crisis2. German 10-year yields fell 4 basis points to 3.38% on safe-haven buying2. And France was not alone:

Belgium’s spread widened more than 10 basis points to 111.28, its highest since 2012; Italy’s rose 10.5 to 123, Greece’s 8.5 to 102 and Spain’s 7.5 to 712. By midday the French yield was still at 5.09%, according to Sharecast4.

The gap. Desk arithmetic: in the week since Moulin spoke, the French yield has gone from “close to 5%”1 to above 5.1%2, and the move on Thursday came while the German yield fell. That is the shape of a country premium, not of a broken market. But Moulin’s own test was fragmentation across the euro area, and on Thursday every spread on the Reuters list widened at once2. One day of that is a mood. A month of it would start to look like the thing he said he was not seeing.

Verdict. The podium holds, for now. Moulin did not promise calm; he set a threshold, and a threshold is more useful to you than a reassurance, because you can check it. Nordea’s reading is the same in other words: unchanged rates next week, a December hike still likely, unless the market turns “clearly disorderly” well beyond France3. The fix Moulin named sits in parliament, not in Frankfurt1. Nothing here is advice.

Sources

  1. ECB's Moulin: No Case for ECB Bond Market Intervention as French Yields Rise — Econostream Media
  2. French debt risk premium reaches euro zone sovereign crisis levels — Reuters via Investing.com
  3. European Central Bank: Communication focus as French spreads widen — FXStreet (Nordea)
  4. Europe midday: Stocks slump as oil rises; Hermes slides on results — Sharecast News

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Ordinary Ledger: the ticket rises, the light one waits
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: The Deutschlandticket goes to €66.80 a month in January. A pay-per-ride version for occasional travellers was taken off the transport ministers' agenda without debate. And the Länder say €14 billion more is needed just to keep today's trains running.
item.content:encoded:
The Deutschlandticket goes to €66.80 a month in January. A pay-per-ride version for occasional travellers was taken off the transport ministers' agenda without debate. And the Länder say €14 billion more is needed just to keep today's trains running.

The transport ministers of the Länder and the federal government closed their autumn conference in Hohenschwangau, in Bavaria, on Thursday2. For your wallet, three lines matter.

The price. From January the Deutschlandticket costs €66.80 a month instead of €631. Desk arithmetic: €3.80 more a month, or 6.0%; €45.60 more over a year, which brings twelve months to €801.60.

The version that did not come. North Rhine-Westphalia and Hamburg wanted a working group on a nationwide “Deutschlandticket light” for occasional travellers: you tap in and out on your phone, and at the end of the month you pay the cheapest fare for the rides you took, capped at the Deutschlandticket price1. NRW already runs such a system, eezy.nrw1. On Wednesday a majority took the motion off the agenda, saying it had been submitted too late1. Bavaria’s minister, Christian Bernreiter, had said beforehand there was no money for it, and the transport operators’ association also opposed it1. NRW’s minister, Oliver Krischer, called it a missed chance and wants it on the next agenda2,3: “Wer nur gelegentlich Bus und Bahn fährt, muss genauso unkompliziert und zu fairen Konditionen unterwegs sein können wie die Vielfahrer”2.

The money behind the trains. The ministers’ resolution asks the federal government to compensate “vollständig”, in full, the extra costs from higher track-access charges that follow an EU Court of Justice ruling and a Cologne administrative court ruling4. And it says that keeping today’s regional rail service alone needs €14 billion more in regionalisation funds by 20314. Bernreiter’s warning is plain: without it, “höhere Ticketpreise und Abbestellung von Verkehren”, higher fares and cancelled services5. Federal transport minister Steffen Bilger came, in dpa’s words, without fresh money5.

The constructive reading. Demand is not the problem: Bavaria says regional rail use in 2024 was 23.8% above 20195. The problem is the invoice for the track, and that is a solvable kind of problem, settled in a budget line rather than a slogan. If you ride rarely, January is a good moment to count your trips against €66.80. Nothing here is advice.

Sources

  1. Hamburg will "Deutschlandticket light" - Entscheidung vertagt — tagesschau.de (NDR)
  2. Länder und Bund informieren über Verkehrsministerkonferenz — dpa-AFX via finanznachrichten.de
  3. "Verpasste Chance": Verkehrsminister vertagen Entscheidung über Deutschlandticket für Gelegenheitsfahrer — Deutschlandfunk
  4. Verkehrsminister machen Druck bei Trassenpreis-Reform — regionalHeute.de (dts Nachrichtenagentur)
  5. Bahnverkehr unter Druck: Länder fordern mehr Geld vom Bund — Neue Presse Coburg (dpa)
