item.title: The fabs are built, and the cash arrives
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Texas Instruments grew revenue 28% and spent less than half as much on plant as a year ago. Free cash flow more than tripled. Some of it was a government cheque, and the release says so.
item.content:encoded:
Texas Instruments grew revenue 28% and spent less than half as much on plant as a year ago. Free cash flow more than tripled. Some of it was a government cheque, and the release says so.

Texas Instruments reported third-quarter revenue of $6.06bn on Wednesday evening, up 28% on a year ago and 11% on the quarter, with net income of $2.43bn1. Chief executive Haviv Ilan credited “continued broad growth in industrial, automotive and data center”1. Analog chips, the unglamorous parts that manage power in everything from cars to servers, grew 32% to $4.91bn2. Both revenue and earnings per share of $2.62 came in above the analyst figures the Wall Street Journal compiled, Quartz reported2.

The dull line. The interesting number is not in the headline. Capital expenditure in the quarter was $463m, against $1.20bn a year earlier; over twelve months it fell to $2.58bn from $4.82bn1. For years TI poured money into 300mm wafer plants. Now the plants are running, and the release says the “benefit of 300mm production” shows up in cash1. Twelve-month cash flow from operations rose 43% to $9.90bn, and free cash flow to $8.42bn from $2.42bn1.

The footnote. Read the definition. TI’s free cash flow is operating cash minus capex plus proceeds from US CHIPS Act incentives, which came to $1.10bn over the twelve months1. A further $469m of CHIPS tax credit sits inside operating cash1. Desk arithmetic: the two together are about 19% of the $8.42bn. TI does not hide this; it prints it in a reconciliation table. That is how a subsidy should look: visible, counted and separable from the business.

The constructive reading. The stockroom is getting leaner, not fatter: finished goods fell to $1.69bn from $1.94bn a year ago, while sales rose1. TI guides to $5.80bn–$6.30bn for the fourth quarter1. In a week when investors are asking whether AI spending will ever pay, here is a chipmaker past its spending phase showing what payback looks like: a lower capex line and a fatter cash line.

Nothing here is advice; it is a reading of a company’s own accounts.

Sources

  1. TI reports third quarter 2026 financial results and shareholder returns — Texas Instruments
  2. Texas Instruments beat earnings expectations on broad-based chip demand — Quartz

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: The WHO calls Ebola a regional test, and counts where people die
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Congo passed 9,700 confirmed cases. The WHO's Africa office says about six in ten recent deaths happened outside treatment centres. That is a statistic about distance and trust, and it can be worked on.
item.content:encoded:
Congo passed 9,700 confirmed cases. The WHO's Africa office says about six in ten recent deaths happened outside treatment centres. That is a statistic about distance and trust, and it can be worked on.

The World Health Organization’s Africa office said on Thursday that the Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak has become a regional public health concern1. “Ebola does not wait. It follows movement, exploits gaps, and tests the strength of our health systems,” regional director Mohamed Yakub Janabi told an online briefing1. “Today, the test is no longer confined to one place.”1

The count. Congo’s health authorities reported 9,704 confirmed cases and 4,687 deaths as of 20 October, a case fatality rate of 48.3%1. The WHO’s weekly report, with data to 19 October, had 9,637 cases and 4,646 deaths2. Desk arithmetic: 67 more confirmed cases and 41 more deaths in one reporting day. The outbreak now covers eight of Congo’s 26 provinces, and 50 of the 66 health zones ever affected reported a new case in the last 21 days1,2. The WHO says its seven-day moving average shows “a modest upward trend”2.

The line that matters. Janabi said about six in every ten recent deaths in Congo occurred outside treatment centres1. That is not a medical fact so much as a logistical one. It means people fall ill and die at home or in ordinary clinics, where nobody can isolate them and where their care exposes relatives and staff.

Beyond Congo. Kenya has nine cases, including one death, and Nigeria one imported case1. The WHO report cites insecurity, displacement and restricted humanitarian access as threats to surveillance2. The Africa CDC will convene health ministers virtually on 28 October1,2.

The constructive reading. The figures are bad, but they are published, daily and by province, which is the precondition for any response. Ministers have a date in the diary, and the WHO has named the specific gap: getting sick people into a bed that is built for this. That is a problem of ambulances, trust and rosters. It is solvable, and it is now on the table in plain numbers.

Nothing here is a reason for readers in Europe to change plans; the figures describe a response, not a risk to you.

Sources

  1. WHO urges coordinated action as Ebola poses regional threat in Africa — Xinhua
  2. Ebola transmission in DR Congo remains active: WHO — Anadolu Agency

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: The court let the students march
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: After his security council, the president said the general recommendation was no demonstrations at all. By two o'clock a Paris judge had suspended a police ban, and the march set off from a hospital gate. That is how a rule of law is supposed to work under pressure.
item.content:encoded:
After his security council, the president said the general recommendation was no demonstrations at all. By two o'clock a Paris judge had suspended a police ban, and the march set off from a hospital gate. That is how a rule of law is supposed to work under pressure.

This morning’s note said the useful document would be whatever the security council admitted had gone wrong. The Elysée published its readout on Thursday. It is short. It says the council reviewed intelligence, anticipation and security for the coming weeks, “while going back over the dysfunctions” behind last weekend’s events1. It does not list them. The admission is now on paper; the inventory is not yet.

The rule for Saturday. Speaking afterwards, President Macron set the line. “The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations,” he said. Unions that still want to march will get “alternative routes proposed by the prefects”; protests by others will be banned “wherever possible”2. He blamed “seditious” ultra-left groups as well as vandals for last Saturday’s riots3. A defence council follows on Friday, “and we will take further decisions,” he said3. Lyon has banned every demonstration on Saturday by decree; Toulon, central Rouen and Grenoble have announced similar bans2.

The machinery. For the interior ministry, Jean-Didier Berger said on BFMTV that Saturday’s deployment will be 20% larger than on 17 October, when about 60,000 police and gendarmes were out3. Desk arithmetic: that is roughly 72,000. Justice minister Gérald Darmanin said 2,500 people have been arrested since the weekend; 174 have been locked up and more than 900 are being prosecuted3. Trials are already under way3.

The check. At 14:25 France 24 reported that an administrative court had suspended a Paris police order banning a student march planned for 2pm by Interfac Île-de-France3. The judge gave no reasons in what was reported3. By 14:53 it reported that the march had set off from the Pitié-Salpêtrière hospital in the 13th arrondissement3.

For you. Don’t read that ruling as a defeat for order. It shows the order working. A ban is an administrative act, and administrative acts can be challenged the same day, by people with a lawyer and a filing. If you plan to be in a French city on Saturday, check your prefecture’s own orders, which differ from city to city2. In Paris, follow what the court allowed, not just what the presidency recommended.

Sources

  1. Conseil de sécurité — Élysée
  2. French weekend protests to be limited to union demos only, says Macron — BBC News
  3. Live: France will ban 'illegitimate' protests in coming days, says Macron — France 24 (with Reuters, AP and AFP)

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Kaub spent a month below the 2018 low
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Eight years ago today the Rhine at Kaub set the low of its reference decade, 25 cm. Every daily mean of the past 31 days has been below it. The storms are coming to the west, not to the Rhine.
item.content:encoded:
Eight years ago today the Rhine at Kaub set the low of its reference decade, 25 cm. Every daily mean of the past 31 days has been below it. The storms are coming to the west, not to the Rhine.

The lowest daily water level the Rhine gauge at Kaub recorded in its 2010–2020 reference period was 25 cm, on 22 October 20182. That was eight years ago today. At 16:15 this afternoon the gauge read 17 cm1,2.

The month. The federal waterways administration publishes the gauge every 15 minutes1. Desk arithmetic on those readings: all 31 daily means from 22 September to 22 October sat below 25 cm. Five were below zero, the lowest a mean of −4.8 cm on 1 October, when the gauge touched −6 cm in the early morning1. The best day was 13 October, at 19.7 cm1. Thursday’s mean so far is 18.2 cm1. The administration flags the readings as raw data, so they can still be revised1.

What the number is. A gauge reading is not the depth of the river. It is measured from a fixed zero, 67.669 m above sea level at Kaub2. The shipping channel is guaranteed to be 1.90 m deep when the gauge reads 77 cm, the “equivalent water level”2. Desk arithmetic: today’s 17 cm is 60 cm short of that reference. Barges load lighter, and more of them are needed for the same tonnage.

The weather. Storm Austen is bringing heavy rain this week, but to Brittany and Normandy, and the winds then shift towards northern France3. That is not the Rhine’s catchment. A river at Kaub is fed by Switzerland, the Black Forest, the Main and the Neckar, and it answers to their rain, not the Channel’s.

The constructive reading. Nothing about this month was hidden. Every reading was public, every quarter of an hour, free to use. Shippers, power stations and chemical plants along the river plan on exactly this data. A low that arrives slowly is one that logistics can price and route around, and the published numbers are what make that possible.

Sources

  1. PEGELONLINE REST API: Kaub (Rhein), water level W, 15-minute raw values for the last 31 days — Wasserstraßen- und Schifffahrtsverwaltung des Bundes (WSV)
  2. PEGELONLINE REST API: Kaub station, current values and characteristic values (NW, MW, GlW, TuGLW) — WSV
  3. Tempête Austen : vents violents ce vendredi sur le nord-ouest du pays — Météo-France

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: A sentence moved the price before the quarter did
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: A merger remark lifted two share prices, and three companies that beat their forecasts fell anyway. Markets grade results against what people were told to expect.
item.content:encoded:
A merger remark lifted two share prices, and three companies that beat their forecasts fell anyway. Markets grade results against what people were told to expect.

On Wednesday, the most expensive sentence on Wall Street was not in an earnings release. After SpaceX posted its first profit as a listed company, Elon Musk said a merger of SpaceX and Tesla would be “a good idea”1. SpaceX closed 7.8% higher. Tesla, which had not yet reported a single number for the quarter, rose 3.4%1. A remark about a deal that does not exist moved a carmaker’s shares more than many quarterly results move a share price.

Then the numbers arrived, and the mood went the other way. Tesla beat forecasts on both lines: 48 cents of adjusted earnings per share against 43 cents expected, and revenue of $28.05 billion against $27.88 billion2. Its shares first rose a little after the close and then slipped, trading about 2–3% lower in the evening1,2. Cboe noted that the fall came before the conference call had even started3. IBM also beat on earnings and revenue; its shares “initially popped” and were last down more than 3%2. Lam Research guided slightly above estimates and dropped more than 5%2. Earlier in the day, AT&T beat, raised its outlook and closed 6.5% lower1.

What the day was measuring. None of this is irrational, and none of it is mysterious. A price is not a verdict on whether a company did well. It is a verdict on whether it did better than the story people had already paid for. Psychologists call that story a reference point: people judge an outcome as a gain or a loss relative to what they expected, not relative to zero. Wednesday showed the two ways a reference point is set. One is the numbers analysts publish before the release. The other is words: a founder’s aside, a guidance range, a rival’s plans.

By the time Tesla reported, the reference point had moved. A 3.4% rise built on a merger remark had already lifted the bar the quarter had to clear. The results beat the analysts’ bar and still fell short of the new one. AT&T is the mirror image. Its quarter was solid by its own accounts, but the reference point was set by a competitor: SpaceX’s plan to turn Starlink into a US mobile carrier5. AT&T’s chief executive answered with plain arithmetic. He told analysts not to “over-rotate on what I would call one carrier of low-band spectrum”5. Arithmetic is slower than a headline. It usually wins in the end, but not on the day.

Relief is measured against fear. Meta offers the third lesson. Its revenue of $64.60 billion beat forecasts and the shares rose about 3% after hours2,4. One prominent analyst called its spending “better controlled than feared”2. Look at the release itself, though. Meta’s 2026 capital spending range is now $135–145 billion, narrowed by raising the floor from $130 billion. Quarterly capital spending was $34.91 billion, and free cash flow was minus $2.12 billion4. The company is also creating a new class of non-voting shares, partly for “capital raising”4. The relief was real, but it was measured against the fear, not against the bill. “Better than feared” is a statement about the mood beforehand, and it says nothing about the cash.

The insurance people buy before the news. The calmest behaviour of the day was the least visible. Before Procter & Gamble reports on Thursday, options traders are pricing a move of about 3% either way, and put contracts at one strike are 1.5 times more active than normal, Cboe noted, “suggesting hedging may be in play”3. Honeywell had four times the usual number of puts at one strike for Friday’s expiry3. People who know that the reference point can move without warning pay a small, known price beforehand to avoid a large, unknown one afterwards. That is not pessimism. It is good housekeeping.

What you can take from it. You do not need to trade anything to use this. When you see “shares fell despite strong results”, there is a question to ask: what was the price measuring itself against? Usually the answer is a sentence: a guidance line, a chief executive’s aside or a rival’s announcement, and you can find it. When you hear “better than feared”, ask what the fear was and then look at the number underneath. Meta’s negative free cash flow was in its own press release4. AT&T’s raised outlook was in the release that preceded a 6.5% fall1,5.

Statements set expectations, but data settles them, and the settling takes longer than a trading day. The useful skill is not to react faster than other people. It is to read the release before you read the reaction. Nothing here is advice.

Sources

  1. Nasdaq leads Wall Street gains as SpaceX, Super Micro boost AI sentiment — Reuters via Investing.com
  2. Stock futures fall as investors digest earnings from Meta and Tesla: Live updates — CNBC
  3. Technology Stocks Pop, Lead Nasdaq Higher — Cboe
  4. Meta Reports Third Quarter 2026 Results — Meta Platforms
  5. AT&T CEO Says SpaceX's Low-Band Spectrum Isn't Cause to 'Over-Rotate' — Stocktwits via Yahoo Finance

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: The index rose, the long rate did not budge
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: The S&P 500 is on course for its best month since April, with the US 10-year yield still at 5.13%. Underneath the index, more Nasdaq stocks hit new lows than new highs.
item.content:encoded:
The S&P 500 is on course for its best month since April, with the US 10-year yield still at 5.13%. Underneath the index, more Nasdaq stocks hit new lows than new highs.

Wall Street closed higher on Wednesday for a third day. The S&P 500 rose 0.58% to 7,757.17, the Nasdaq Composite 1.05% to 26,702.86 and the Dow 0.69% to 52,856.091. Cboe notes the S&P 500 is now on its best pace for a monthly gain since April, and the VIX volatility index fell 3.6% to below 172. The trigger was a pair of results that eased worries about AI spending: SpaceX’s first profit as a listed company and a stronger outlook from Super Micro Computer, which rose 9.6%1.

What did not move is the price of time. The US 10-year Treasury yield closed at 5.13% on 21 October, against 4.19% on the first trading day of the year3. It first closed at 5% on 15 September and has stayed at or above that level on every day since except three, peaking at 5.31% on 5 October3.

A rally against a 5% long rate is not impossible; it simply asks more of earnings, because future profits are discounted harder. That is why Wednesday was sorted by income statements, not by the bond market. It also explains how narrow the day was. On the Nasdaq, 53 stocks set new 52-week highs and 216 set new lows; on the NYSE the count was 131 highs against 221 lows1. Volume, 16.11 billion shares, was below the 20-session average of 17.10 billion1.

The night was less cheerful. After Meta, Tesla, IBM and Lam Research reported, S&P 500 futures fell 0.5% and Nasdaq-100 futures 0.7%, and Asia opened lower, with the Hang Seng down more than 2%4. One good day is a data point, not a trend; the yield line is the trend. Nothing here is advice.

Sources

  1. Nasdaq leads Wall Street gains as SpaceX, Super Micro boost AI sentiment — Reuters via Investing.com
  2. Technology Stocks Pop, Lead Nasdaq Higher — Cboe
  3. Daily Treasury Par Yield Curve Rates, 2026 — U.S. Department of the Treasury
  4. Stock futures fall as investors digest earnings from Meta and Tesla: Live updates — CNBC

item.title: Ten ships and a letter to Washington
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: The full count for Wednesday came in at ten AIS-visible crossings of the Strait of Hormuz. Overnight Iran's foreign minister set out his terms in a newspaper. One of those is a ledger, the other an opening bid.
item.content:encoded:
The full count for Wednesday came in at ten AIS-visible crossings of the Strait of Hormuz. Overnight Iran's foreign minister set out his terms in a newspaper. One of those is a ledger, the other an opening bid.

Yesterday evening this desk counted nine ships by mid-afternoon. The complete UTC day closed at ten AIS-visible commercial crossings of the Strait of Hormuz: six into the Gulf and four out, one of them a tanker and nine cargo ships1. The tanker was a small products carrier, 105 metres long, bound for the UAE1. The average since 19 October is 5.7 crossings a day, against a pre-crisis baseline of 84.81. Desk arithmetic: ten crossings is about 12% of a normal day.

The method, again. The counter sees only ships that broadcast their position; its counts “miss ships running dark”, and it leaves out small craft, of which nine more crossed on Wednesday1. The official comparison, IMF PortWatch, has still not published anything after 18 October1. So ten is a floor, and a floor that moved up.

The letter. Overnight Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, took his case to a Western newspaper. “Iran is prepared to give diplomacy another chance if we see strong evidence of a sincere desire on the part of the US,” he wrote in the Financial Times, as reported by Bloomberg2. The price of that evidence is specific: lift the naval blockade and return to the Islamabad memorandum signed in June, under which Iran was to reopen the strait and the US was to lift the blockade, release frozen oil funds and remove sanctions2. “If they adhere to these conditions, they should know that the Strait will be fully opened,” he said in an earlier interview with Iraqi media2. In that interview he also claimed Washington had accepted Iran’s conditions for a seven-day reopening plan but wanted extra clauses; the US has not confirmed his account3.

The other side of the table. Bloomberg notes that the US has shown “little appetite” to return to the June memorandum, and that President Trump has suggested he may restart bombing after the 3 November midterms2. Brent rose above $110 a barrel on Wednesday2.

Why this matters to you. Your fuel bill does not read op-eds; it reads tanker crossings and insurance quotes. A minister naming conditions in public is useful, because conditions can be met or refused on the record. But until the visible count climbs for days in a row, the strait is open in print and narrow in fact. Nothing here is advice.

Sources

  1. Strait of Hormuz traffic on Wednesday 21 October 2026 — hormuz.now
  2. Iran tells US to prove it wants peace by lifting blockade — The Business Times (Bloomberg)
  3. Araghchi Says U.S. Accepted Conditions for Seven-Day Hormuz Plan, Sought Additions — EconoTimes

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: The Annex: letter a has no date
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Germany's new tobacco tax law, read in the Federal Law Gazette itself. The mistake everyone is talking about sits in one short article; the reason it bites sits in a single letter of the tariff.
item.content:encoded:
Germany's new tobacco tax law, read in the Federal Law Gazette itself. The mistake everyone is talking about sits in one short article; the reason it bites sits in a single letter of the tariff.

Today’s annex is the document itself: the law amending Germany’s tobacco tax act, dated 19 October 2026 and published in the Federal Law Gazette, issue 2026 I No. 309, on 20 October1. It runs to three pages and three articles. It is signed by President Steinmeier, Chancellor Merz and Finance Minister Klingbeil1.

Article 3. The clause in the headlines is one sentence: “Dieses Gesetz tritt am Tag nach der Verkündung in Kraft” (“This law enters into force on the day after its promulgation”)1. There is no second paragraph and no separate date for the new rates1. So everything in the law took effect on 21 October2.

Why that matters: letter a. Article 1 replaces the tariff in §2(1). For cigarettes, letters b to e each begin with a period: 1 January to 31 December 2027, then 2028, 2029, and 1 January 2030 to 14 February 20311. Letter a has no period. It sets 18.57 cents per cigarette plus 21.05% of the retail price “vorbehaltlich der Buchstaben b bis e”, meaning “subject to letters b to e”1. Read literally, letter a covers every day that b to e do not, and that includes the rest of 2026. The 2027 rate under letter b is 14.34 cents1. Desk arithmetic: the text as printed would tax a cigarette this autumn 4.23 cents more than next year. Fine-cut tobacco and cigars follow the same pattern1.

What the text meant. The rest of the law points one way. Article 1 also allows new tax stamps to be bought five weeks before a change in the tariff, and Article 2 sets stamp-ordering rules that run “bis zum 31. Dezember 2026”1. Customs gives that as the reason for early entry into force: to allow time to make and order new stamps2. Its notice says the old rates apply unchanged until 31 December 20262.

The repair route. The finance ministry wants to use §61 of the federal ministries’ joint rules of procedure, which covers “printing errors and obvious inaccuracies”. After a law has been passed, that needs the consent of the presidents of the Bundestag and the Bundesrat3. The ministry says the error was already in its own draft3. That is why the Cologne constitutional lawyer Markus Ogorek, quoted by Die Welt, doubts the route: “In any case, this is not a mere printing error in the Federal Law Gazette,” he said, because the gap was already in the government draft and parliament did not correct it; and a parliamentary amending law would be the “legally certain way”3.

The receipt so far. No correction had been published in issues up to No. 313 on 21 October3, and by 05:13 on Thursday the Gazette’s site had no issue 3144.

The reading. Strip out the embarrassment, and this is a three-page law with one missing date in letter a and one clause, Article 3, too short to rescue it. The fix will also be a document. Read it when it arrives, and check which of the two routes it took.

Sources

  1. Gesetz zur Änderung des Tabaksteuergesetzes vom 19. Oktober 2026 (BGBl. 2026 I Nr. 309) — Bundesgesetzblatt / Federal Ministry of Justice
  2. Tabaksteuer - Klarstellung zum Inkrafttreten — Zoll (German customs administration)
  3. Finanzministerium will Tabaksteuer-Panne ohne neues Gesetz beheben — Außenlage
  4. Bundesgesetzblatt Teil I, Nr. 313 (latest issue online; Nr. 314 not yet published) — Bundesgesetzblatt

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: The wind came back to the auction
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Thursday's German power cleared at €148.61 a megawatt hour, 30% below Wednesday. Nobody gave a speech about it. The forecast simply had twice as much wind and sun in it.
item.content:encoded:
Thursday's German power cleared at €148.61 a megawatt hour, 30% below Wednesday. Nobody gave a speech about it. The forecast simply had twice as much wind and sun in it.

Germany’s day-ahead power auction cleared Thursday’s delivery day at an average of €148.61 per megawatt hour, according to the Bundesnetzagentur’s SMARD data1. Wednesday’s delivery day had cleared at €211.941. Desk arithmetic: that is a fall of about 30% in a single day, and the cheapest day since 11 October (€122.31)1.

What changed. Not gas, not a summit, not a speech. The forecasts that the auction runs on changed. SMARD’s day-ahead forecast for Thursday puts onshore wind at about 634 gigawatt hours, against about 237 for Wednesday; wind and solar together come to about 920 GWh, against about 4212. Desk arithmetic: forecast wind and solar cover roughly 70% of Thursday’s forecast consumption of about 1,319 GWh, against roughly 31% on Wednesday2. When more hours are met by wind, fewer are set by a gas plant, and the average falls.

What did not change. One windy day does not make a cheap month. Over 1 to 22 October the daily price has averaged €168.96, against €95.54 for the same days of 20251. Desk arithmetic: about 77% higher. September averaged €144.821. The chart’s shape is the one this desk showed yesterday: a calm spring and early summer, then an autumn that costs more1.

Why it matters to you. Most households do not buy at the day-ahead price; they buy through a supplier that hedges months ahead. What the auction shows is the cost of the marginal hour, and how much of that the weather can still take off. The case for grids and interconnectors rests on exactly this: a windy Thursday in the north is worth more if the power can travel. Nothing here is advice.

Sources

  1. Market data: day-ahead wholesale price, Germany/Luxembourg (filter 4169), daily — Bundesnetzagentur / SMARD.de
  2. Market data: forecast generation (wind onshore, wind offshore, photovoltaics) and forecast consumption, Germany, daily — Bundesnetzagentur / SMARD.de

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Podium vs Print: "quite close to 2%" depends on the ruler
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: A Bank of Japan deputy governor told parliament that underlying inflation is quite close to target, and argued for more rate rises. The bank's own six staff measures for August run from 1.3% to 2.6%. He is right on average, and the average is the argument.
item.content:encoded:
A Bank of Japan deputy governor told parliament that underlying inflation is quite close to target, and argued for more rate rises. The bank's own six staff measures for August run from 1.3% to 2.6%. He is right on average, and the average is the argument.

The podium. On Wednesday Ryozo Himino, a deputy governor of the Bank of Japan, told parliament that “underlying inflation is quite close to 2% and will likely converge to levels consistent with our price target”1. He added that financial conditions “remain accommodative” even after last month’s rate rise, and that “delaying necessary adjustment to monetary support” could let inflation risks materialise1. In plain words: more rises are coming, and the case rests on that one phrase about underlying inflation.

The print. “Underlying” is not one number. The bank’s own research staff publish six measures that strip out different kinds of noise, from fresh food and energy to policy effects such as subsidies and free school lunches2. For August, the latest month available, they range from 1.3% to 2.6%2:

The broad measures, which exclude fresh food and institutional factors, sit at 2.6% and, without energy, 2.2%2. The trimmed mean, which drops the most extreme price changes at both ends, is 2.2%2. The narrower measures are lower: 1.8% excluding all food and energy, a weighted median of 1.5% and a mode of 1.3%2. The trend is rising, though. The trimmed mean was 1.7% in May and has gone up each month since2.

The gap. Desk arithmetic: the simple average of the six is 1.93%, which is indeed “quite close to 2%”. But three measures are at or above 2.2% and three are below 2%, and the low ones describe the typical price change, not the loud ones. Himino’s other argument is about pressure still to come: fuel and raw material costs, and “brisk global AI demand” boosting exports and investment1. The trade print released the same morning complicates that. September exports were up 16.7% on a year earlier, well short of the 20.1% analysts had expected, the second monthly slowdown in a row, although chip shipments rose 49.4%3.

Verdict. The podium is fair about the middle and quiet about the spread. That is not a trick; it is what a committee does when it has to reduce six rulers to one decision. For you, the useful habit is to look at which ruler a speaker picks. A central bank that wants to keep raising rates will point at the measures above 2%, and the ones below 2% will be the first thing it is asked about if the next prints soften. Nothing here is advice.

Sources

  1. BOJ's Himino signals readiness to raise borrowing costs — Reuters via Investing.com
  2. Indicators for Core CPI (research data, XLSX) — Bank of Japan
  3. Japan exports post huge miss in September as growth slows to 16.7% — CNBC

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Ordinary Ledger: the new contract pays first
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Gas for a household signing today costs 28% more than in January; electricity 6% more. People in running contracts have not felt it yet, says the industry's own count. The letter is the thing to watch.
item.content:encoded:
Gas for a household signing today costs 28% more than in January; electricity 6% more. People in running contracts have not felt it yet, says the industry's own count. The letter is the thing to watch.

The energy industry association BDEW’s latest price check carries data as of 20 October1. Its headline is short: rising prices for households “am aktuellen Rand”, at the current margin1.

The figures. A gas contract that a single-family household can sign today averaged 14.2 cents per kilowatt hour on 15 October, 3.1 cents or 28% more than at the start of the year1. Electricity for a household using 3,500 kWh a year averaged 39.3 cents, 2.1 cents or 6% more1. For customers in running tariffs, whose prices were usually set at the turn of the year or fixed, BDEW says there has been no effect “bislang”, so far1.

The ledger. Desk arithmetic, at BDEW’s reference volumes: 20,000 kWh of gas at the new-contract average costs about €2,840 a year, €620 more than at January’s price. 3,500 kWh of electricity costs about €1,376, €73.50 more. Grid fees add a little in January: Verivox estimates about €19 a year for that gas household and about €8 for a 4,000 kWh electricity household, with large regional differences, Berlin among the steepest3.

What protects you. A supplier must tell you of a price change at least a month before it applies, give the reason and the size, and point out your right to terminate early2. A price guarantee in the contract can rule an increase out, though often only for the parts the supplier controls2. If you are in the basic supply, the Grundversorgung, you can leave with two weeks’ notice at any time2. Desk arithmetic: a change for 1 January has to be announced by about 1 December.

The constructive reading. The gap between the new price and the running one is time, and time is useful. It is the window in which to find your contract, note the end date and read every letter from your supplier, including the ones that look like advertising, which the regulator warns can hide increases2. Nothing here is advice.

Sources

  1. Quick-Check Gas- und Strompreise: Aktuelle Preise und Vergleich zu 2021/2022 — BDEW Bundesverband der Energie- und Wasserwirtschaft
  2. Preise und Abschläge — Bundesnetzagentur
  3. Gaskunden müssen mit höheren Netzentgelten rechnen — tagesschau.de (rbb24)

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Meta spent more on buildings than its business brought in
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Meta's third-quarter revenue beat forecasts by more than a billion dollars. Its free cash flow was negative for the quarter, and it announced a new class of non-voting shares to help pay for what comes next.
item.content:encoded:
Meta's third-quarter revenue beat forecasts by more than a billion dollars. Its free cash flow was negative for the quarter, and it announced a new class of non-voting shares to help pay for what comes next.

Meta reported third-quarter revenue of $64.60 billion on Wednesday, up 26% on a year earlier and ahead of the $63.37 billion analysts had expected, according to CNBC1,2. Its shares rose about 3% in extended trading2. That is the podium version. The cash-flow statement tells a plainer story.

The cash. Meta’s operating activities brought in $32.79 billion in the quarter1. Its capital expenditures, including principal payments on finance leases, were $34.91 billion1. Free cash flow, the difference, was minus $2.12 billion, against plus $10.63 billion a year earlier1. Desk arithmetic: purchases of property and equipment rose from $18.83 billion to $33.94 billion, an increase of about 80%1. Meta ties the spending to the computing capacity it has and “what is scheduled to come online”1. For one quarter, building it cost more than the business generated.

The balance sheet. None of this is distress. Meta ended September with $82.45 billion in cash and marketable securities1. But long-term debt stood at $80.92 billion, up from $58.74 billion at the end of 2025, and net property and equipment rose from $176.4 billion to $253.2 billion over the same nine months1. Headcount fell 15% to 66,7751. Fewer people, more concrete.

The new share class. Meta’s board approved a new class of listed, non-voting Class C shares, to be issued as a one-for-one stock dividend once the change takes effect on 19 January 20271. The company names “capital raising” first among the reasons, alongside pay and possible acquisitions, and says the scale of investment the AI race demands is “significant”1. Meta says the stock dividend “will not change the voting power of any shareholder”, and the board presents the change as a way to keep the “founder-led model”1.

The outlook. Meta narrowed its 2026 capital-spending range to $135–145 billion, from $130–145 billion, and said it would keep “investing aggressively” next year without giving a figure1. Desk arithmetic: nine-month spending was about $85.8 billion, so the range implies roughly $49–59 billion in the fourth quarter alone1. The quarter’s results also include a $9.89 billion charge for a settlement with US state attorneys general over teen mental health1.

The constructive reading: a company with an advertising business growing 26% can afford to build. The question for the next few quarters is not whether Meta can pay, but how long it is willing to pay more than it earns in cash. Nothing here is advice.

Sources

  1. Meta Reports Third Quarter 2026 Results — Meta Platforms (investor relations)
  2. Stocks making the biggest moves after hours: Meta Platforms, Tesla, Lam Research, IBM & more — CNBC

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: North Kivu treats one Ebola patient in three outside an Ebola centre
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Congo's latest situation report has 509 patients in hospital in North Kivu and 410 places in its treatment and transit centres. The other provinces have empty beds. The outbreak's next problem may be logistics more than medicine.
item.content:encoded:
Congo's latest situation report has 509 patients in hospital in North Kivu and 410 places in its treatment and transit centres. The other provinces have empty beds. The outbreak's next problem may be logistics more than medicine.

The Congolese health ministry’s situation report for 19 October, published on 20 October, recorded 85 new confirmed cases of Bundibugyo Ebola, bringing the total since the outbreak began to 9,637, with 4,646 deaths1. That is the headline line. The more useful line is on page seven, under case management1.

The beds. In North Kivu, 154 patients were admitted on 19 October and 95 left, ten of them cured1. That leaves 509 patients in hospital, 58 of them children under five1. The province’s Ebola treatment and transit centres were 81.0% full, with 332 patients for 410 places; suspected-case beds were 86.5% full1. And 177 patients, or 34.8%, were being cared for in ordinary health facilities that are not Ebola centres1. The report lists that among its “défis”, its challenges1.

The other provinces. The picture elsewhere is the opposite. Ituri, which still accounts for 72.7% of all confirmed cases, had 431 patients and an occupancy rate of 42.5%1. Haut-Uélé had 29 patients for 169 beds (17.2%) and Tshopo 13 for 36 (36.1%)1. Bas-Uélé is the exception, with its three beds for confirmed patients all taken and 47 people in isolation while a proper centre at Buta’s general hospital is still not ready1. Nationally, the tracker that compiles the bulletins counts 982 patients for 1,630 beds, or 60 per 1002.

Why it matters. Desk arithmetic: North Kivu took 59 more patients than it discharged in a single day. Each patient treated outside a dedicated centre is harder to isolate, and Ebola spreads through the bodily fluids that a ward has to contain. The province is also behind on the other side of the work: 79.7% of its 19,316 contacts were seen that day, below the 95% the response requires, and only 9 of 22 “rings” of disinfection and follow-up around new cases had been opened1.

The constructive reading. Laboratories are keeping up: 514 samples were analysed on 19 October, 16.5% of them positive1. Across all provinces, 3,184 alerts came in and every one was checked and classified1. The surveillance machinery is doing its job, and the bottleneck has moved downstream, to beds, ambulances and staff in one province. That is a better problem than not knowing where the cases are. It is a problem solved by trucks, tents and rosters rather than by speeches, which is why the next bulletins’ page seven is the one to read.

Nothing here is a reason for readers in Europe to change plans; the figures describe a response, not a risk to you.

Sources

  1. Rapport de situation de la 17e épidémie de la maladie à virus Ebola / RDC, SitRep N°158 (report date 19 Oct, published 20 Oct) — Institut National de Santé Publique (DRC), archived by ebola-tracker.org
  2. DRC Ebola, 19 October 2026: 9,637 confirmed cases (SitRep 158) — ebola-tracker.org

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Paris closed its squares from eight to eight
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Demonstrations are banned in central Paris and Lyon on Thursday. At ten, the president sits down with the intelligence services to go over what went wrong on 17 October. The orders are precise; the review is the part that will last.
item.content:encoded:
Demonstrations are banned in central Paris and Lyon on Thursday. At ten, the president sits down with the intelligence services to go over what went wrong on 17 October. The orders are precise; the review is the part that will last.

The Paris police prefecture has issued an order banning gatherings and demonstrations in parts of the capital on Thursday from 08:00 to 20:001. The map is long and specific. It covers the Elysée, Matignon, the National Assembly and the Senate. It also covers the Champs-Elysées, the Louvre, the department-store district, the Place d’Italie, Bastille and République, the Châtelet–Halles shopping area, the Ile de la Cité and the Paris railway stations1. In Lyon, the Rhône prefect banned a march planned for Thursday afternoon by the student union Unef and the NPA1. Its route would have ended at Place Bellecour, where violence broke out on Saturday and a tourist office branch was set on fire1.

The review. At 10:00 President Macron chairs a security council with Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu and the intelligence services2. The Elysée says it will cover intelligence, anticipation and security plans for the coming weeks, “while going back over the dysfunctions” that led to last weekend’s events2. That is an unusual sentence for a presidency to publish. It admits that something in the machinery failed, and it commits to looking at it. Speaking in Qatar on Wednesday, Mr Macron called the meeting a chance to draw up a “compte rendu”, an account, of the weekend2.

Saturday. The next test is 24 October. The government has promised a large police presence, armoured vehicles and the elite GIGN, BRI and Raid units, and more bans on demonstrations are expected3. Shopkeepers are worried. Between 2,000 and 3,000 shops were looted or damaged last weekend, and many plan to keep their shutters down3. “Concern is at its highest,” said Pierre Bosche of the Confédération des commerçants de France3. Justice minister Gérald Darmanin put the number of people jailed at 1743.

For you. If you are in Paris on Thursday, the order is about gatherings and demonstrations in named places, for twelve hours, and the main railway stations are on the list1. Several countries, including the United States, China and Germany, have advised their citizens in France to be careful3. Check the prefecture’s order for the exact streets, not a national headline.

The useful document today is not the ban. It is whatever the security council admits went wrong, and whether it is written down.

Sources

  1. France en direct : des manifestations interdites, les partis reçus à Matignon — France 24 (with AFP and Reuters)
  2. Emmanuel Macron présidera un conseil de sécurité jeudi matin, en présence de Sébastien Lecornu et des services de renseignement, annonce l'Elysée — franceinfo
  3. Violences : les partis reçus à Matignon, le renseignement convoqué à l'Elysée — France 24 (AFP)

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Austen was named before it arrived
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Britain's Met Office named the autumn's first storm two days ahead and raised an amber warning for Cornwall a day ahead. France has fourteen départements in yellow for Thursday. A warning that comes early is the cheapest kind.
item.content:encoded:
Britain's Met Office named the autumn's first storm two days ahead and raised an amber warning for Cornwall a day ahead. France has fourteen départements in yellow for Thursday. A warning that comes early is the cheapest kind.

The Met Office named Storm Austen on Tuesday morning, two days before it was due1; Ouest-France calls it the first storm of the autumn4. An Atlantic low is expected to deepen rapidly as the jet stream feeds it, and to cross southern Britain late on Thursday and through Friday morning1,2.

The British warnings. On Wednesday the forecaster raised an amber wind warning for the whole of Cornwall, the Isles of Scilly and parts of West Devon, inside a wider yellow warning from Thursday evening into Friday2. “Winds gusts could potentially reach 60-70 mph for a time,” said deputy chief forecaster Chris Bulmer2. Rain adds to it: 20–30 mm in many places, more on high ground in the west1. The Met Office expects winds to ease through Friday afternoon, with more unsettled weather and possibly further warnings at the weekend2.

The French warnings. Météo-France’s bulletin for Thursday, issued at 16:01 on Wednesday, has 14 départements in yellow and none in orange or red3. Wind runs from Brittany and the Channel coast to Var, the Alpes-Maritimes and Corsica; Finistère, Morbihan, Loire-Atlantique and Pas-de-Calais are also yellow for rain and flooding, and Gard is still yellow for river floods3. The rain-flood yellow runs from 02:00, with a lull expected between 14:00 and 18:005. In Loire-Atlantique the wind warning starts at 21:00, and Ouest-France quotes a Météo-France forecaster saying all coasts from Brittany to Hauts-de-France and the Atlantic seaboard will see wind4.

The constructive reading. Nothing in either bulletin is extraordinary yet: an amber in one corner of England, yellows in France2,3. That is the system working as designed. A name and a colour two days early give councils time to clear drains, ferry operators time to reschedule and you time to tie down the garden furniture. The expensive storms are the ones nobody was told about.

Sources

  1. Storm Austen named — Met Office
  2. Amber warning issued as Storm Austen approaches — Met Office
  3. Vigilance météo et crues pour jeudi 22 octobre — Météo-France
  4. Des rafales de vent attendues dès jeudi soir sur le littoral de Loire-Atlantique avec le passage de la tempête Austen — Ouest-France
  5. Pluie-inondation : voici les 4 départements placés en vigilance jaune ce jeudi — CNEWS

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: The law said today. The customs office said January.
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Germany's tobacco tax law came into force on Wednesday by mistake, more than two months early on paper. Within hours the customs administration had published what still applies, and the finance ministry had started a correction. The error is embarrassing; the repair is the part worth watching.
item.content:encoded:
Germany's tobacco tax law came into force on Wednesday by mistake, more than two months early on paper. Within hours the customs administration had published what still applies, and the finance ministry had started a correction. The error is embarrassing; the repair is the part worth watching.

On Tuesday the federal law raising Germany’s tobacco tax was published in the Federal Law Gazette. It sets out steps up in the tax for 2027 to 20301. Its final clause reads: “This law enters into force on the day after its promulgation”2. That day was Wednesday, 21 October 20261. Read literally, the higher rates applied from this morning, more than two months before anyone intended.

The finance ministry confirmed the error on Wednesday. Bild had reported it first2. A spokesman called it a technical mistake in the date of entry into force2. At the government press conference, the ministry added a detail that matters more than the apology: the error was already in its own draft bill, and it was not caught anywhere in the procedure, in government or in parliament2,3. Asked how many people had read the text, the ministry said the number of hands and eyes could not be counted on two hands3.

What the machinery did next. The striking thing is not the slip. Long laws carry slips. It is the order in which the repair arrived. On the day of publication, the customs administration, which collects the tax, put a notice on its website. It called the clause an “obvious inaccuracy” and stated plainly what applies1. The rates in force on 19 October continue unchanged until 31 December 20261. The new tariff for cigarettes, fine-cut, heated tobacco and substitutes starts on 1 January 2027, and for cigars, cigarillos, pipe and water-pipe tobacco on 1 March 20271. The notice also explains why the law entered into force early at all: so that the new tax stamps can be designed and ordered in time1.

That is a small document doing a large job. Anyone at a tobacco wholesaler, a kiosk or a tax office who wanted to know what to do on Wednesday morning did not need a minister. They needed a dated notice from the authority that sends the bills, and it was there.

The legal argument. At the press conference the finance ministry said the will of the legislator was clear from the law itself3. The explanatory memorandum names 1 January 2027 in 13 places, the ministry said, and the amended section 2 of the tobacco tax law begins each time with “for the period from 1 January 2027”3. The ministry said it is aiming to use the correction procedure under §61 of the joint rules of procedure of the federal ministries, so that the Bundestag does not have to vote again, because the error is obvious3. It also said it was working on instructing the administration not to collect the higher rates3. Details were not yet settled on Wednesday3.

Asked who was responsible, government spokesman Stefan Kornelius pointed to the ministry that drafts the text; the chancellery coordinates, he said, and the federal president checks constitutionality3.

The industry’s view. The tobacco makers were relieved and cross. Maximilian van Ackeren of the VdR, a tobacco industry association, called it “dilettantism”2. Jan Mücke of the BVTE, another industry association, warned that the sector would spend weeks “in a grey zone” tolerated by the authorities and asked for legal certainty quickly2. Both points are fair. Tolerance is not the same as law, and a correction that takes weeks would leave honest firms technically on the wrong side of a statute.

What is actually at stake. Tagesschau notes that the reform could raise the price of a pack of 20 cigarettes by about four euros to €11.78 by 20302. The tax is expected to bring in about €1.5 billion extra next year, against €17.6 billion collected in 20252. None of that changes because of the slip. What changes is a few weeks of paperwork.

A second correction, same room. The same press conference produced a quieter repair. This desk reported this morning that the “more than €220 billion” announced at Tuesday’s investment summit was a total for the year, not a summit haul. On Wednesday the economy ministry gave the exact figure, €228.6 billion. It covers large investment projects of €100 million or more announced by companies during 20263. Some were announced at the summit, but not all, and the ministry said it has no figure for the share that is new3. That is less impressive than the headline, and more useful: you now know the method.

The argument. Two numbers were wrong or loose on Tuesday, and both were made precise on Wednesday, on the record, in answer to plain questions. That is how institutions are supposed to work. A free press asks; a ministry answers; an agency publishes a notice that a shopkeeper can read. You will hear more today about embarrassment. The better story is the speed of the repair. Watch whether the correction is formally published, and how soon. That will be the receipt.

Sources

  1. Tabaksteuer - Klarstellung zum Inkrafttreten — Zoll (German customs administration)
  2. Ministerium unterläuft Panne beim Gesetz zur Tabaksteuer — tagesschau.de
  3. dts-Mittagsreport: Regierungspressekonferenz vom 21.10.2026 — dts Nachrichtenagentur

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Europe was sorted by receipts, not moods
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: A Ray-Ban maker jumped about 15% and a supermarket chain fell about 14% on the same Wednesday morning. Both moves came from quarterly figures, and one of them priced the French curfews into a forecast.
item.content:encoded:
A Ray-Ban maker jumped about 15% and a supermarket chain fell about 14% on the same Wednesday morning. Both moves came from quarterly figures, and one of them priced the French curfews into a forecast.

By early afternoon on Wednesday the pan-European STOXX 600 was up 0.7%, after a session on Tuesday in which it fell as much as 1% before ending virtually flat1. Germany’s DAX was up 1% and France’s CAC 40 0.8%; London’s FTSE 100 was largely flat after UK inflation rose more than expected to 3.5%1. Index levels are the least interesting part of the day. The spread between individual shares told you more.

The top of the list. EssilorLuxottica, which makes Ray-Ban glasses, rose more than 15% after third-quarter revenue beat expectations1. Adidas gained 2.5% after raising its full-year outlook1. European chip-equipment makers BE Semiconductor, ASM International and ASML, and the chipmaker STMicroelectronics, each rose more than 2%1.

The bottom. Carrefour fell nearly 14% after cutting its annual forecast and saying that riots, looting and curfews had raised costs and disrupted trading1. That is the French unrest arriving where it eventually has to: in a company’s guidance, written in euros. A curfew is a public order measure. For a retailer it is also shorter opening hours, extra security and damaged stock.

The expectations bar. Analysts polled by Reuters expect third-quarter earnings at STOXX 600 companies to grow 20.7% from a year earlier, slower than the 24.0% of the second quarter but still fast1. More than half of the index by market value reports over the next two weeks1. A high bar makes results matter more, in both directions, as Wednesday showed.

Across the Atlantic. Wall Street opened higher: the Dow up 0.30% at 52,652.85, the S&P 500 up 0.31% at 7,736.43 and the Nasdaq up 0.67%, helped by results from SpaceX and Super Micro Computer2. Netflix slipped after its forecast failed to impress2. Meta and Tesla report after the close1. Nothing here is advice; it is a reading of the day’s published figures.

Sources

  1. European shares edge up on earnings support; Big Tech results awaited — Investing.com
  2. Wall St opens higher as SpaceX, Super Micro results lift AI stocks — Investing.com (Reuters)

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Nine ships and a fire off Bukha
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: A tanker was hit by an unknown projectile near the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday morning, and by mid-afternoon an open ship-tracking counter had logged nine commercial crossings for the day. Both facts are true, and neither is the whole picture.
item.content:encoded:
A tanker was hit by an unknown projectile near the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday morning, and by mid-afternoon an open ship-tracking counter had logged nine commercial crossings for the day. Both facts are true, and neither is the whole picture.

On Wednesday a tanker was struck by “an unknown projectile” about 11 nautical miles off Bukha, on Oman’s side of the Strait of Hormuz, the UK Maritime Trade Operations centre said1. A fire broke out and the ship is “now at anchor”1. “All crew are reported as safe. There is no reported environmental impact at this time,” UKMTO said1. TradeWinds, the shipping paper, says fresh incidents have pushed the confirmed tally of Iranian attacks beyond 30 vessels in three weeks3. AFP notes that attacks have increased as Washington escorts more ships through the strait1.

The counter. Hormuz.now, a site that counts commercial crossings from ships’ public AIS signals, had logged nine crossings by 14:26 UTC on Wednesday: five into the Gulf and four out, one of them a small products tanker2. Its rolling seven-day average is 2.3 crossings a day, against a pre-crisis baseline of 84.82. The ships it saw today were mostly bulk carriers and general cargo, bound for ports such as Jebel Ali, Sohar and Umm Qasr2.

Read the method before the number. The site is candid about what it misses. Its counts are “AIS-visible only and miss ships running dark”, and it excludes small craft; six of those crossed by the same hour2. A ship that switches off its transponder to avoid being targeted does not appear. So the counter is a floor, not a total. The official comparison, IMF PortWatch, publishes several days late; its latest day is 18 October2.

Why this matters to you. Fuel and freight prices in Europe still lean on this water. A floor of nine visible ships tells you the route is not working normally; it does not tell you it is closed. A fire tells you the risk is real; it does not tell you traffic has stopped. When two careful sources disagree, the gap is usually method, not malice.

The constructive habit is the same as this morning: take the count with its footnote. The day the visible number rises for a week in a row, without fires, that will be the news.

Sources

  1. Ship attacked near Strait of Hormuz: maritime agency — Arab News (AFP)
  2. Strait of Hormuz traffic on Wednesday 21 October 2026 — hormuz.now
  3. Greek and Kuwaiti product tankers identified as latest targets in Gulf attack — TradeWinds

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: The nurse lost the test, and the patients still got better
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: A Stockholm trial pitted a few nurse visits against guided self-help therapy for stress. The therapy did better, the nurses failed the statistical bar they were set, and both groups were markedly less stressed a year later.
item.content:encoded:
A Stockholm trial pitted a few nurse visits against guided self-help therapy for stress. The therapy did better, the nurses failed the statistical bar they were set, and both groups were markedly less stressed a year later.

Researchers at Karolinska Institutet randomly assigned 172 primary-care patients in Stockholm with mild-to-moderate stress-related ill health to one of two routes1. Eighty-five got nurse-led collaborative care: two to six visits over up to twelve weeks, built on problem-solving, explanation and care coordination1. Eighty-seven got guided self-help cognitive behavioural therapy: twelve weekly modules with support from a psychologist, online or as a book with sessions1. The study was published in BMJ Mental Health and summarised by Medscape on Wednesday1.

The test the nurses failed. The question was whether the nurse route was “not worse” than the therapy by more than a set margin. It was not shown to be: the difference favoured the therapy (effect size 0.22), and the upper end of its confidence interval, 0.52, overshot the 0.3 margin1. That is a precise way of saying the trial cannot rule out that the nurses’ route is meaningfully weaker.

The numbers both groups share. On the ten-item Perceived Stress Scale, the nurse group fell from 24.9 to 19.4 at twelve weeks and the therapy group from 25.8 to 18.41. A year later the scores were 16.3 and 15.21. Desk arithmetic: that is a drop of 8.6 points for the nurse route and 10.6 for the therapy, measured from where each group started. Patients in the nurse group needed on average 3.68 sessions1.

What the study cannot say. There was no untreated group, so part of the improvement may be time itself1. It was one centre, and most participants were middle-aged, well-educated women1. Satisfaction ratings were similar in both arms1.

The constructive reading. The authors’ own conclusion is modest: the nurse route is “safe, relatively easy to administer” and may still be useful in primary care1. That is the kind of finding that rarely makes a headline and often makes a service work. Not every patient needs the best-scoring option on day one; many need a competent first step that is available this month.

Sources

  1. Nurse-Led Collaborative Care Falls Short of Guided CBT for Stress, but Both Improve Symptoms — Medscape

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Podium vs Print: cheap power has not reached Germany's auction yet
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: An ECB blog published on Wednesday says renewables are pulling wholesale electricity prices down in many countries. Germany's day-ahead auction says October has so far cost about 80% more than the same days last year. Both are true, and the gap between them has a name: grids.
item.content:encoded:
An ECB blog published on Wednesday says renewables are pulling wholesale electricity prices down in many countries. Germany's day-ahead auction says October has so far cost about 80% more than the same days last year. Both are true, and the gap between them has a name: grids.

The podium. On Wednesday three ECB economists published a long blog post on why the euro area has withstood this year’s energy shock better than feared1. One passage is about electricity. “The expansion of renewable generation capacity is reducing wholesale electricity prices in many countries,” they write, because more renewables mean fewer hours in which a gas plant sets the price1. The evidence they cite is specific. In Spain the share of hours in which gas set the price fell from around 80% in 2020 to just above 20% in the first nine months of 2026; in France it fell from around 60% to around 20%1. Unlike in 2021–22, they say, the latest shock hit countries with more renewable and nuclear power less hard1.

The print. Germany’s day-ahead auction tells the other half. The daily average price for the Germany-Luxembourg zone was €169.93 per megawatt hour over 1 to 21 October 2026, against €94.14 for the same days of 20252. Desk arithmetic: that is about 80% higher. Wednesday’s delivery day cleared at €211.942. September averaged €144.82, with a high of €256.55 on 14 September2.

The gap. The two are not contradicting each other as much as it looks. The blog does not name Germany, and its claim is about structure, measured over years1. The auction is about this autumn, in one bidding zone, on days when the wind and the sun decide how often gas is needed at the margin. The chart shows the shape plainly: through the spring and early summer, months after the shock began, German power mostly stayed between about €77 and €110; it was the autumn, with a second wave of higher gas prices, that lifted it1,2.

Verdict. The podium is right about the direction, and the print is right about the bill. What closes the gap is in the same blog post: “further integration of EU electricity markets, including more cross-border interconnections and investment in grids”, so that cheaper renewable electricity “could flow where it is needed”1. That is dull machinery: cables, substations, permits. It is also the only part of the argument that turns a Spanish average into a German invoice. Nothing here is advice.

Sources

  1. Resilience of the euro area economy – weathering one shock, preparing for the next — European Central Bank (The ECB Blog)
  2. Market data: day-ahead wholesale price, Germany/Luxembourg (filter 4169) — Bundesnetzagentur / SMARD.de

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Britain printed 3.5%, and most of it came through the pump
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: UK inflation rose to 3.5% in September on motor fuels, while core prices moved less. The euro area showed the same split a week ago. Eight days before the ECB decides, the useful number is the second one.
item.content:encoded:
UK inflation rose to 3.5% in September on motor fuels, while core prices moved less. The euro area showed the same split a week ago. Eight days before the ECB decides, the useful number is the second one.

The Office for National Statistics said on Wednesday that consumer prices rose 3.5% in the 12 months to September, up from 3.1% in August and the highest rate since October 20251. Investing.com called it more than expected, and London’s FTSE 100 lagged the continent in the morning3.

Where it came from. Transport made the largest upward contribution, “particularly motor fuels”1. Petrol averaged 169.5 pence a litre in September, up 8.2p in a month and the highest since August 2022; diesel averaged 192.5p, up 10.7p, the highest since July 20221. Motor fuel prices were 29.8% higher than a year earlier1. Heating oil (kerosene) rose 22.7% in the month1.

Where it did not. Core inflation, which leaves out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, rose from 2.6% to 2.8%1. Food inflation stayed at 1.3%, the lowest since 20211. Services rose from 3.4% to 3.7%, partly on air fares, which fell less in September than a year earlier1. Desk arithmetic: the gap between headline and core is 0.7 percentage points.

The same picture in Frankfurt’s data. The euro area showed the split more sharply. Headline HICP was 3.8% in September; core was 2.5%2. Desk arithmetic: a gap of 1.3 points. The ECB’s deposit rate is also 2.5%, after rises in June and September2. Lagarde told the IMF’s steering committee last week that wages have “so far shown no material response to the energy shock”2.

What to take from it. A fuel shock shows up first in the headline and only later, if at all, in the core. The chart shows the deposit rate now level with core inflation, and the headline line well above both. That is the position the Governing Council takes into its meeting on 29 October. Britain’s print adds a second witness, not a new verdict. Nothing here is advice; it is a reading of published numbers.

Sources

  1. Consumer price inflation, UK: September 2026 — Office for National Statistics
  2. IMFC Statement by Christine Lagarde, President of the ECB, Bangkok, 17 October 2026 — Bank for International Settlements
  3. European shares edge up on earnings support; Big Tech results awaited — Investing.com

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Ordinary Ledger: the occasional rider waits
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: This morning the Länder transport ministers were to discuss a monthly cap for people who ride the bus now and then. By the afternoon the motion had been taken off the agenda, on a majority vote, for arriving too late. The idea is not dead. It is unfiled.
item.content:encoded:
This morning the Länder transport ministers were to discuss a monthly cap for people who ride the bus now and then. By the afternoon the motion had been taken off the agenda, on a majority vote, for arriving too late. The idea is not dead. It is unfiled.

The proposal was called “Bundesweiter elektronischer Gelegenheitstarif”, a nationwide electronic tariff for occasional riders1. According to BR, citing people in the room, the Länder transport ministers took it off the agenda of their conference in Hohenschwangau on Wednesday by majority decision, because it had been submitted too close to the meeting1.

What was on the table. North Rhine-Westphalia and Hamburg proposed a smartphone check-in, check-out fare: you register the start and end of each trip, the cheapest fare is worked out automatically, and in a month you never pay more than a Deutschlandticket1,2. That ticket costs €63 a month and rises to €66.80 in January2.

Who said what. Bavaria’s transport minister Christian Bernreiter, who chairs the conference, had said before the session that there was certainly no money for it, with billions already missing, for example to order regional trains1. The association of German transport companies, the VDV, also rejected the idea1. Social welfare associations welcomed it as cheaper mobility for poorer people1.

The ledger. Desk arithmetic: the January step is €3.80 a month, or €45.60 over a year for a full-year holder2. The proposed cap would have tied the occasional rider’s worst month to the same number. Tonight there is no such cap, and nothing has changed for anyone’s fare.

The constructive reading. A procedural reason is the cheapest kind of no. It says nothing about the merits and invites a better-prepared motion. The ministers stay until Thursday, mostly on funding, with low water in German rivers and autonomous driving also on the programme1. If the money argument is serious, that is the room in which to put a euro figure next to it.

Sources

  1. "Deutschlandticket light" kommt vorerst nicht — tagesschau.de (BR24)
  2. Deutschlandticket nach Bedarf? Verkehrsminister planen Ticket für Gelegenheitsfahrer — tagesschau.de

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: A data centre that arrives on a truck
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Nvidia's new DSX Pod puts seven Vera Rubin racks, pre-cabled and liquid-cooled, into a container of about 28 tonnes. The claim is that a site can start serving in 14 days instead of six months. The bottleneck it attacks is not chips but building work.
item.content:encoded:
Nvidia's new DSX Pod puts seven Vera Rubin racks, pre-cabled and liquid-cooled, into a container of about 28 tonnes. The claim is that a site can start serving in 14 days instead of six months. The bottleneck it attacks is not chips but building work.

At its GTC conference in Berlin on Wednesday, Nvidia announced the DSX Pod AI Factory: seven of its Vera Rubin AI racks packed into a unit roughly the size of a standard shipping container, weighing about 28,000 kilograms, and designed to travel by truck on normal roads1. The cabling and liquid cooling are assembled at the factory1.

What is actually new. Not the chips. The change is where the work is done. “The only thing that has to happen when it gets to the site is it’s placed in its location, connected to the rest of the other containers, and validated through final burning and testing,” Ian Buck, Nvidia’s vice president of hyperscale computing, told reporters1. Nvidia says this cuts the time for a new AI data centre to start serving tokens from six months to 14 days1. That figure is the company’s own and is untested until the first pods arrive.

Why Europe gets a mention. Nvidia said the pod is for customers worldwide and could help with deployment problems faced by European customers1. It did not spell out which. What the design does is move the cabling and cooling work from the site into a factory hall, where it can be done in series and checked before the unit leaves1.

What it does not change. A pod still has to be placed, connected to the other containers and tested on site1, and the site still needs its power connection; that does not come on the truck. Nvidia gave no price; analysts estimate a single Vera Rubin rack at more than $7 million1. Deliveries are expected from early 2027 through manufacturing partners including Foxconn, Gigabyte, Lenovo, HPE, Quanta and Pegatron1.

The direction of travel. Nvidia has moved from selling single graphics chips to servers, then racks, and now containers of racks1. Jensen Huang said recently that what Nvidia sells into one gigawatt of data-centre capacity has gone from about $18 billion to “$40-plus billion per gigawatt”1. The investor question this week, as Meta and Tesla report, is whether buyers keep spending at that rate2. The engineering question is simpler and more useful: how much of a building can be made in a factory.

Sources

  1. Nvidia announces plug and play Vera Rubin racks that can be shipped on a truck — CNBC
  2. European shares edge up on earnings support; Big Tech results awaited — Investing.com

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: Nigeria is the fifth country, and the clock started on 11 October
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Nigeria has confirmed its first case of Bundibugyo Ebola, a woman who travelled from Uganda. Nine days passed between her visit to a clinic in Abuja and a laboratory result. Those nine days are now the work.
item.content:encoded:
Nigeria has confirmed its first case of Bundibugyo Ebola, a woman who travelled from Uganda. Nine days passed between her visit to a clinic in Abuja and a laboratory result. Those nine days are now the work.

Nigeria has confirmed its first case of Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus, the World Health Organization said on Wednesday1. The patient is a woman who had recently travelled from Uganda. She developed symptoms on 7 October, four days after arriving, sought care at a private health facility in Abuja on 11 October, and was confirmed by laboratory testing on 20 October1. She is in isolation and receiving care1.

The nine days. Desk arithmetic: 11 October to 20 October is nine days between her first visit to a clinic and a confirmed result. That gap is where contacts accumulate. Nigerian authorities have so far identified 44 contacts under monitoring, and infection control is being strengthened at the clinic where she was seen1. The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention has activated its incident management system, and WHO is supplying protective equipment and help with tracing1.

The wider picture. Nigeria is the fifth country to detect the disease since the outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo was declared in mid-May1. The ECDC counts 9,552 confirmed cases and 4,602 deaths in the DRC, from data to 18 October2. There is no licensed vaccine or specific treatment for this species1. WHO has not recommended any restrictions on travel or trade, and asks countries in the region to keep a high level of readiness1.

For readers in Europe. The ECDC’s modelling still puts the risk of importation into the EU/EEA at very low, even in a pessimistic scenario, though sporadic imported cases cannot be excluded2. Nothing here is a reason to change your plans.

The constructive reading: a new country is bad news, but a case found, isolated and surrounded by a list of 44 names is the system catching up. Watch the list, not the map.

Sources

  1. WHO supports Nigeria after first Ebola case confirmed — UN News
  2. Ebola disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo — ECDC

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: The curfew moved to eleven
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Paris and Lyon renewed their night-time restrictions for Wednesday night, and Lyon's now starts two hours later. The justice minister counted 2,500 people taken into custody since the violence began. Attention shifts to Saturday.
item.content:encoded:
Paris and Lyon renewed their night-time restrictions for Wednesday night, and Lyon's now starts two hours later. The justice minister counted 2,500 people taken into custody since the violence began. Attention shifts to Saturday.

The Paris police prefecture has issued new orders for Wednesday night. They “prohibit the presence of adults as well as minors” in the République and Halles areas from 23:00 until 06:00 on Thursday1. In Lyon, the Rhône prefect renewed the curfew and the ban on gatherings, but it now starts at 23:00 instead of 21:001. That is the most useful line of the day: the authorities are giving back two hours of the evening because the previous nights were calm.

The count. Justice minister Gérald Darmanin, visiting Marseille, said there had been 2,500 police custody cases since the violence began, and 174 people have been sent to prison for handling stolen goods or assault1. He said most of them had no criminal record1. Those are the numbers of a justice system working through a backlog, and they will keep rising for a while after the streets go quiet.

Saturday. The weekend is the test. The yellow-vest coordination has filed a route for Saturday from Bastille to Opéra; the police prefecture had not confirmed it by Wednesday morning1. Interior minister Laurent Nuñez has sent instructions to prefects, including to ban gatherings “likely to disturb public order”1. In Toulon, the Var prefect banned face coverings in public from Wednesday 14:00 to Monday 09:00, set a Saturday curfew for unaccompanied minors and banned demonstrations in the city centre for that day1. Toulouse’s Ligue 1 match was moved from Saturday to Sunday at the prefecture’s request1.

The tone at the top. Speaking from Doha, President Emmanuel Macron said a state of emergency was not needed and that the measures in place had brought calm back since Monday1. He will meet the intelligence services on Thursday morning for a detailed account of 17 October1.

For you, if you live in or are travelling to a French city this week: the rules are set by local orders, street by street, and they change daily. Read the prefecture’s order for your area rather than a national headline.

Sources

  1. DIRECT. Violences du 17 octobre: des couvre-feux à Paris et Lyon renouvelés ce mercredi soir — BFMTV

Commentary for information only. Not advice.

item.title: The Annex: the point of return, read line by line
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: UNEP's Emissions Gap Report 2026, out today in Nairobi, says 1.5°C will be passed and sets out what it would take to come back below it. Read as a document, it is a ledger of required cuts against pledged ones, with a column of things that already worked.
item.content:encoded:
UNEP's Emissions Gap Report 2026, out today in Nairobi, says 1.5°C will be passed and sets out what it would take to come back below it. Read as a document, it is a ledger of required cuts against pledged ones, with a column of things that already worked.

Today’s annex is the UN Environment Programme’s Emissions Gap Report 2026, “The Point of Return”, published in Nairobi on Wednesday and read here through UNEP’s own release1.

What it assumes. That global warming will pass 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels1. The question it asks is narrower: what is the “lowest possible” overshoot? Its answer is a path on which warming peaks at 1.7–1.8°C around mid-century and returns to or below 1.5°C by 2100, with about a 50% chance1.

What that path costs in emissions. Global greenhouse gas emissions would have to fall 18% by 2030, 45% by 2035 and 69% by 2040, all against 20251. Full implementation of national pledges, the NDCs, would give 5–8% by 2030 and 11–15% by 20351. The required rate is 5.7% a year for 2025–2035, faster than the roughly 5% in the IPCC’s earlier pathways1.

What happens without it. Current policies point to 2.8°C this century; delivered pledges to 2.6°C1. UNEP says both are worse than last year’s projections because of the United States’ withdrawal from the Paris Agreement and revised estimates of historical emissions1. Every five years of CO2 at current levels adds about 0.1°C to peak warming1.

The column that already worked. More than 220 policy evaluations are cited. Electricity-sector policies cut emissions by an average of 9%; carbon taxes and cap-and-trade schemes by 5–13%1. Since the Paris Agreement, global renewable capacity has grown three times faster than anticipated and solar seven times faster1. If that continues, with additional policy, the world would be on track to triple renewable capacity by 20301.
